schema_notes.is_historical_867: True if the barony name is contemporarily attested as a settlement, fortress, or administrative unit by <= 867 CE.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: True if the barony name directly adopts a specific proper hydronym, oronym, choronym, or named topographic feature (excluding directional/locator compounds).
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Records attested pre-867 CE names for the same site or immediate predecessor when distinct from the barony name.

b_naissos.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Claudius Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150–161 CE) as Naissus (Ancient Greek: Ναϊσσός), one of the four major cities of Roman Dardania.
b_naissos.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ancient Paleo-Balkan hydronym Naissos (the Nišava River), attested in Greek as Ναϊσσός (Naissós) and Latin as Naissus; transmitted into South Slavic as Niš (with Proto-Albanian-like or regional late antique phonetic development).

current_repo_state.name: Nîsch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_svrljig.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as a župa and settlement in the 1019–1020 charters of Byzantine Emperor Basil II (Eparchy of Niš) as Sfeligovos.

morphemes.translation: etymology uncertain (possibly Slavic *svelug 'all forest', *vrljugati 'to wind', or Latin spelunca 'cave')

b_svrljig.etymology_analysis: Medieval Serbian/Bulgarian župa first attested in 1019–1020 CE; its etymology is debated, with proposals linking it to Slavic *vrljugati ('to wind/meander'), *svelug ('all forest'), or Latin spelunca ('cave').

b_pirot.first_mention_attestation: The name Pirot is first mentioned in 1443 CE (or 1498 CE in local Serbian records), though the Roman way-station Turres is attested in the 3rd-century Tabula Peutingeriana and Byzantine Quimedava by Procopius in the 6th century CE.

morphemes.translation: possibly from Greek pyrgos ('tower') or Slavic pir ('feast')

b_pirot.etymology_analysis: The modern toponym Pirot appears in the 15th century (1443 CE), likely continuing or adapting Byzantine Pyrgos ('tower', translating Roman Turres), though the exact derivation remains debated.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tabula Peutingeriana (3rd century CE, as Turres); Procopius (6th century CE, as Quimedava)
older_name_by_867.notes: Turres ('towers') stood on the Via Militaris; replaced by Byzantine Quimedava and later medieval Pirot.

b_breznik.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 11th-century Story of Isaiah (Bulgarian Apocryphal Chronicle) as БР(Ѣ)ЗНИКЪ (Breznik), already described as a city.
b_breznik.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Bulgarian/South Slavic word breznik ('birch forest/grove'), from breza ('birch') + locative/collective suffix -nik; cognate with Czech Březník.

b_ohrid.first_mention_attestation: The Slavic name Ohrid first appeared in 879 CE (at the Fourth Council of Constantinople), succeeding the ancient Greek/Illyrian name Lychnidos (first mentioned 353 BCE).
b_ohrid.etymology_analysis: Commonly derived from the South Slavic phrase *vo hridi ('on/in the cliff'), referring to the fortified hill rising above Lake Ohrid; attested from 879 CE onward.

current_repo_state.name: Lîchnit
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ancient Greek sources (353 BCE, as Λυχνιδός / Lychnidos)
older_name_by_867.notes: From Greek lychnos ('light/lamp'); remained the standard name until replaced by Slavic Ohrid in 879 CE.

b_bitola.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Bitola inscription of 1015 CE (under Tsar Ivan Vladislav / Gavril Radomir of the First Bulgarian Empire) as a fortified city.
b_bitola.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Church Slavonic ѡ҆би́тѣл҄ь (obitělь, 'monastery, cloister, abode'), losing its initial vowel o- when the original meaning became opaque (cf. its Greek/Turkish name Monastir).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Founded by Philip II of Macedon (mid-4th century BCE, c. 359–336 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Heraclea Lyncestis flourished through late antiquity before being abandoned after Slavic raids in the 6th century CE.

b_devol.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 1019 CE Greek charter of Byzantine Emperor Basil II as Δεάβολις (Deabolis), corresponding to Slavic Дѣволъ (Devol), a major fortress in Kutmichevitsa.

morphemes.translation: medieval fortress and river name (etymology uncertain)

b_devol.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1019 CE as Byzantine Greek Δεάβολις (Deabolis) and Old Church Slavonic Дѣволъ (Devol); likely of pre-Slavic or early Slavic origin associated with the Devoll River valley.

b_kastoria.first_mention_attestation: While Procopius (6th century CE) used Kastoria for the lake, the first reference to the town of Kastoria is by John Skylitzes regarding events of the late 10th century CE.
b_kastoria.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Greek Καστοριά (Kastoria), meaning 'place of beavers', derived from καστόρι (kastori, 'beaver'), which inhabited Lake Orestiada/Kastoria.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Livy (199 BCE, as Celetrum); later Diocletianopolis (c. 300 CE) and Procopius (6th century CE, Justinianopolis)
older_name_by_867.notes: Celetrum was in Orestis; Justinian I relocated Diocletianopolis onto the peninsula in the 6th century CE.

b_goritsa.first_mention_attestation: The urban core of Korçë (historically Goritsa) dates back to the late 15th century CE (founded by Ottoman nobleman Ilias Bey Mirahori); no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_goritsa.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic Gorica (Bulgarian/Macedonian Горица, 'little mountain/hill'), diminutive of gora ('mountain'), adapted into Albanian as Korçë and Greek as Korytsa.

b_melnikpirin.first_mention_attestation: Though the region entered the First Bulgarian Empire under Khan Presian (836–852 CE), the town of Melnik itself is first attested in written sources in the 11th century CE.
b_melnikpirin.etymology_analysis: English CK3 localisation renders b_melnikpirin as 'Pirin' (the nearby mountain range, linked to Slavic Perun or Thracian Perinthos), while the town of Melnik (repo name Melnîch) is named from Old Bulgarian мел (mel, 'white clay, chalk') + -nik.

current_repo_state.name: Melnîch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_scaptopara.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the famous 238 CE Latin and Koine Greek inscription (petition of the Scaptoparans to Emperor Gordian III), on a Hellenistic Thracian settlement dating to c. 300 BCE.
b_scaptopara.etymology_analysis: Ancient Thracian toponym Σκαπτοπάρα (Scaptopara), containing the Thracian element -para ('market town/village'); modern Blagoevgrad was later known as Gorna Dzhumaya before 1950.

b_vranje.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in Anna Komnene's Alexiad regarding events of 1093 CE (seized by Serbian Grand Prince Vukan).

morphemes.translation: swarthy, black, dark (or personal name Vran)

b_vranje.etymology_analysis: Derived from the South Slavic adjective vran ('dark, black, raven-colored') or the archaic Slavic personal name Vran.

current_repo_state.name: Wranje
current_repo_state.b_origin: Vranje (ancient South Slavic settlement in the South Morava valley) (in-game: Wranje)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Constituent capital seat disambiguated from Morâwe.

b_glubocica.first_mention_attestation: The župa of Glbočica/Dubočica is first mentioned in the 12th century CE as a possession of the Nemanjić dynasty (while Leskovac itself is first mentioned in a 14th-century charter of Stefan Dušan).
b_glubocica.etymology_analysis: Glubočica (later Dubočica) derives from Old Slavic *glǫbokъ ('deep') + -ica, referring to the deep basin/valley of the South Morava around Leskovac.

b_novobrdo.first_mention_attestation: Founded and fortified in the late 13th century CE under Serbian King Stefan Uroš II Milutin as a major silver-mining town and fortress.
b_novobrdo.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Serbian/South Slavic toponym meaning 'New Hill', calqued in medieval Latin as Novus Mons / Monte Novo and German/Saxon as Nyeberghe.

current_repo_state.name: Nîenberch
current_repo_state.b_origin: Novo Brdo (Slavic novo-brdo, 'New Mountain / Mining Hill') (in-game: Nîenberch)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Descriptive South Slavic toponym calqued to Tarraconian Nîenberch.

b_morava.first_mention_attestation: The medieval city of Morava (Greek: Μοράβος), built on the site of Roman Margum, is first attested as an episcopal seat in 879/880 CE.
b_morava.etymology_analysis: Named after the Great Morava River (Slavic adaptation of ancient Margus), renewed in the 9th century on the ruins of Roman Margum.

current_repo_state.name: Morâwe
current_repo_state.b_origin: Morava (ancient Great Morava settlement / Braničevo) (in-game: Morâwe)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Ancient Slavic regional centre on the Great Morava.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman sources (Battle of the Margus, 285 CE; Treaty of Margus, 435 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Margum on the Moesian Limes was destroyed by Avars/Slavs in the early 7th century and renewed as Slavic Morava in the 9th century.

b_skopje.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Claudius Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) as Scupi (Ancient Greek: Σκοῦποι), a major city of Roman Dardania.

morphemes.translation: ancient settlement name (transmitted via Slavic Skopje / Albanian Shkup)

b_skopje.etymology_analysis: Attested in Latin as Scupi and Greek as Σκοῦποι (Skoupoi), likely of Illyrian/Paeonian origin, transmitted into South Slavic as Skopje and Albanian as Shkup.

current_repo_state.name: Skûpi
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_zegligovo.first_mention_attestation: The medieval župa of Žegligovo (modern Kumanovo region) is first mentioned in 14th-century Serbian charters, notably the 1355 CE charter of the monastery of Arhiljevica.

morphemes.translation: medieval regional/župa name (etymology obscure; modern Kumanovo from Cumans)

b_zegligovo.etymology_analysis: Žegligovo is a medieval Slavic župa name attested in 14th-century Serbian charters (1355 CE); the modern town Kumanovo derives from the Cumans who settled in the 12th century.

b_tetovo.first_mention_attestation: Tetovo was founded in the 14th century CE on the site of the ancient town of Oaeneon (Οαινέον).

morphemes.translation: possessive/toponymic formation (traditionally linked to Slavic personal name Teto/Htet)

b_tetovo.etymology_analysis: Founded in the 14th century CE, likely derived from a Slavic personal name (*Teto/*Htet) + possessive suffix -ovo; known in Ottoman Turkish as Kalkandelen.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Livy 43.19 (169 BCE); Tabula Imperii Romani / Greek Oaeneon (Οαινέον)
older_name_by_867.notes: Attested as Oaeneum/Oaeneon in Roman antiquity before medieval Tetovo emerged in the 14th century.

b_veles.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Veles is attested from the 11th century CE (First Bulgarian Empire / Byzantine charters), succeeding ancient Paeonian Bylazora (annexed by Philip V in 217 BCE) and Greek Velissos.

morphemes.translation: ancient toponym Velissos adapted by Slavs (folk-etymologized with Slavic god Veles)

b_veles.etymology_analysis: Reflects a Slavic adaptation of the ancient Greco-Paeonian name Velissos (Βελισσός), later associated in folk etymology with the Slavic deity Veles.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Polybius / Classical sources (Paeonian city Bylazora, annexed by Philip V of Macedon in 217 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Bylazora was the largest Paeonian city before Roman/medieval Veles.

b_kicevo.first_mention_attestation: First attested under its medieval name in 1018 CE in a document of Byzantine Emperor Basil II as Kitzabis (Byzantine Greek: Κίτζαβις).

morphemes.translation: medieval settlement name (attributed to Slavic Berziti tribe)

b_kicevo.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1018 CE as Byzantine Greek Κίτζαβις (Kitzabis) and Slavicized as Kičevo, succeeding the ancient Illyrian/Penestae settlement of Uskana.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Livy / Polybius (Third Macedonian War, 171–169 BCE, as Uskana / Ωξάνα)
older_name_by_867.notes: Uskana was inhabited by the Penestae and contested during the Third Macedonian War.

b_prilep.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Greek as Πρίλαπον (Prilapon) in 1014 CE as the place where Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria died after the Battle of Kleidion.
b_prilep.etymology_analysis: From Old Slavic pri- + lep ('stuck on [the rock]'), describing the medieval fortress clinging to the rocky hilltop above the Pelagonian plain.

b_strumica.first_mention_attestation: The Slavic name Strumica appears in written sources in the 11th century CE (captured by Byzantine commander David Arianites in 1016 CE), though the town is attested since the 2nd century BCE as Astraion and in Roman times as Tiberiopolis.
b_strumica.etymology_analysis: Named after the Strumica River (a tributary of the Struma, from Thracian Strymón < PIE *srew- 'stream'), adopted by the Slavic Strymonites tribe.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 2nd century BCE Greek sources (Αστραίον / Astraion) and Roman-era Tiberiopolis (Τιβεριούπολις)
older_name_by_867.notes: Astraion ('starry') was renamed Tiberiopolis under the Roman Empire before receiving the Slavic name Strumica.

b_shtip.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 2nd century BCE by Polyaenus as Astibos (river/coronation site of Paeonian kings), and as the Roman settlement Estipeon under Tiberius (14–37 CE).
b_shtip.etymology_analysis: Evolved from ancient Paeonian Astibos (originally the Bregalnica River) to Roman/Byzantine Estipeon/Stipeon, and into South Slavic Štip via Proto-Albanian phonetic rules (Shtip).

b_maleshevo.first_mention_attestation: Local tradition and secondary summaries place the earliest mention of Berovo/Maleševo in the 11th century CE; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_maleshevo.etymology_analysis: Derived from the South Slavic personal or tribal name Maleš + possessive suffix -evo, designating the Maleševo mountain region around Berovo.

b_prosek.first_mention_attestation: The medieval fortress of Prosek (Greek: Πρόσακου) is attested in 1019 CE in Emperor Basil II's charter (and later as the 13th-century seat of Dobromir Chrysos and Strez).
b_prosek.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic prosek ('gorge/cut-through', translating earlier Greek Stenae 'gorge'), referring to the Vardar gorge later called Demir Kapija ('Iron Gate') in Ottoman Turkish.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tabula Peutingeriana (4th century CE) and Classical Greek tradition (Στεναί / Stenae)
older_name_by_867.notes: Fortified since the Paeonian and Macedonian periods; Prosek is the medieval Slavic calque/successor.

b_velbazhd.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned under the Slavic name Velbazhd (Велбъжд) in a 1019 CE charter of Byzantine Emperor Basil II.
b_velbazhd.etymology_analysis: Medieval Slavic name Velbazhd (meaning 'camel' in Old Church Slavonic; Latin Velebusdus, Greek Belebousda). Modern Kyustendil was named later after 14th-century Serbian magnate Constantine Dragaš (Kösten + Turkish il).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman-era inscriptions and coins (1st–2nd century CE, Ulpia Pautalia under Hadrian)
older_name_by_867.notes: Important Roman city in Dacia Mediterranea before being renamed Velbazhd in the Middle Ages.

b_bosilegrad.first_mention_attestation: Earliest surviving historical and ecclesiastical records for the Bosilegrad area date to the Ottoman period (early 17th-century churches such as St. Nicholas in Božica and Ottoman fiscal registers); no pre-867 CE attestation exists.
b_bosilegrad.etymology_analysis: South Slavic compound of bosil (either 'basil' or a personal name) + grad ('town/fortress').

b_kratovo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned under its current name Kratovo in 1330 CE (during the Serbian medieval period).
b_kratovo.etymology_analysis: Widely linked to its setting inside the crater of an extinct volcano (Greek krater + Slavic suffix -ovo).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman-era Dardania mining settlement Tranatura (c. 3rd–4th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman fortifications and mines existed at Tranatura before medieval Kratovo was attested in 1330 CE.

b_adrianopolis.first_mention_attestation: Refounded and renamed Hadrianopolis (Ancient Greek: Ἁδριανούπολις) by Roman Emperor Hadrian c. 125 CE on the site of Orestias and Thracian Uskudama.
b_adrianopolis.etymology_analysis: Named after Roman Emperor Hadrian (117–138 CE) + Greek polis ('city'); adapted into Ottoman Turkish as Edirne and South Slavic as Odrin.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eutropius, Breviarium 6.10 (Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus's capture of Uscudama, 72–71 BCE) and Greek Orestias tradition
older_name_by_867.notes: Hadrian rebuilt and expanded Orestias/Uskudama into Hadrianopolis c. 125 CE.

b_mezeshka.first_mention_attestation: Mezek Fortress (Mezeshka krepost; Byzantine Neutzikon) was constructed in the 11th–12th centuries CE.
b_mezeshka.etymology_analysis: Adjectival form of Mezek (Bulgarian Мезешка крепост, Mezeshka krepost), an 11th–12th century Byzantine-Bulgarian fortress known in Greek as Neutzikon.

b_didymoteichon.first_mention_attestation: The name Didymoteichon (Greek: Διδυμότειχον) first appears in written sources in 591/592 CE, following Justinian I's refortification of the city.
b_didymoteichon.etymology_analysis: From Byzantine Greek Διδυμότειχον (Didymóteichon, 'twin wall'), referring to the double fortifications built under Justinian I; later shortened to Dimotica/Dimetoka.

b_beroe.first_mention_attestation: The ancient Thracian settlement of Beroe (5th–4th century BCE) was refounded/fortified by Philip II of Macedon in 342 BCE.

morphemes.translation: ancient Thracian city name (later Slavicized as Boruy)

b_beroe.etymology_analysis: Ancient Thracian toponym Beroe (renamed Ulpia Augusta Traiana by the Romans and Irenopolis in 784 CE by Empress Irene; Slavicized as Boruy, later Ottoman Eski Zagra / Stara Zagora).

b_janitsa.first_mention_attestation: Arises in the early 15th century CE (Ottoman documents as Yenice-i Zağra, built on/replacing a Slavic settlement called Janitsa); no pre-867 CE attestation exists.
b_janitsa.etymology_analysis: Janitsa reflects the Slavicized form of Ottoman Turkish Yenice ('new town', Yenice-i Zağra, i.e. Nova Zagora) from the 15th century CE.

b_haskovo.first_mention_attestation: A fortress was built in the 9th–10th century (traditionally dated c. 985 CE, with Haskovo celebrating its 1,000th anniversary in 1985); the Eski Mosque dates to 1395 CE.
b_haskovo.etymology_analysis: From Ottoman Turkish Hasköy (has 'imperial estate/pure' + köy 'village'), with köy replaced by the Bulgarian toponymic suffix -ovo.

b_burgas.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned under the name Burgas in the 13th century CE by Byzantine poet Manuel Philes (succeeding an earlier medieval watchtower Pyrgos and nearby Roman Deultum).
b_burgas.etymology_analysis: Derived from Greek πύργος (pyrgos, 'tower') via Byzantine/Ottoman Turkish Burgaz (with alternative proposals linking it to Gothic baurgs or Thracian pyurg).

current_repo_state.name: Burchas
current_repo_state.b_origin: Burgas / Pyrgos (ancient Greek watchtower fortress) (in-game: Burchas)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Constituent capital seat of Burgas disambiguated from ancient Apollonia Pontica / Sozopol.

b_sozopol.first_mention_attestation: The name Sozopolis (Σωζόπολις) began appearing in written records by the 1st century CE (and bishops are recorded from 431 CE), succeeding the 7th-century BCE Milesian colony Antheia / Apollonia Pontica.
b_sozopol.etymology_analysis: From Greek Σωζόπολις (Sozopolis, 'City of Salvation'), replacing pagan Apollonia Pontica in the early Christian/Roman period.

current_repo_state.name: Sôsôpel
current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Apollonia Pontica / Sozopolis (founded 610 BC on the Black Sea) (in-game: Sôsôpel)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Ancient 7th-century BC Milesian colony Apollonia Pontica.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Founded c. 610 BCE by Milesian colonists as Antheia, soon renamed Apollonia
older_name_by_867.notes: Apollonia Pontica was sacked by Rome in 72 BCE and later Christianized as Sozopolis.

b_potamuskastel.first_mention_attestation: Built in the late 5th–early 6th century CE, the fortress flourished in the 9th–10th centuries CE under the name Potamukastel (Byzantine Greek Potamoukastellon).
b_potamuskastel.etymology_analysis: From Byzantine Greek Ποταμουκάστελλον (Potamoukastellon, 'River Castle'), situated near Sredets (formerly Karabunar) in Burgas Province.

b_kran.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned under its modern name in 1190 CE, when surviving Byzantine troops retreated to Kran en route to Beroia (though archaeological remains include a 7th–8th century Byzantine fortification).

morphemes.translation: medieval fortress name (etymology uncertain; possibly Thracian substrate)

b_kran.etymology_analysis: Medieval Bulgarian fortress and despotate capital attested from 1190 CE; the name Kran (Крън) is of uncertain, possibly pre-Slavic Thracian origin.

b_sliven.first_mention_attestation: While inhabited since antiquity and medieval times, Sliven is first explicitly documented in a 1792 CE Ottoman register (as Sliven Sanjak / İslimiye); no pre-867 CE attestation of the name Sliven exists.
b_sliven.etymology_analysis: From Slavic sliv ('confluence', referring to the confluence of three rivers in the valley) + suffix -en; known in Turkish as İslimiye and Greek as Sílymnos.

b_kopsis.first_mention_attestation: Constructed in the first half of the 12th century CE; Kopsis (Greek: Κωψίς) is attested as the capital of Voysil and Radoslav's domain in the late 13th century CE.
b_kopsis.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortress near Anevo/Karlovo (also called Anevo Fortress), built in the 12th century CE and attested in Byzantine Greek as Κωψίς (Kopsis).

b_dbilin.first_mention_attestation: The Bulgarian form Dbilin (Дбилин) is attested in 14th-century inscriptions/sources (1357 CE), evolving from Byzantine Diampolis / Diocletian's Diospolis (293 CE) and ancient Thracian Kabyle (341 BCE).
b_dbilin.etymology_analysis: Dbilin is the 14th-century Bulgarian phonetic evolution of Byzantine Diampolis, itself from Diospolis (293 CE, named for Zeus and Emperor Diocletian), which later became Yambol.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Demosthenes (341 BCE, as Kabyle); Diocletian (293 CE, as Diospolis)
older_name_by_867.notes: Kabyle was conquered by Philip II in 341 BCE, expanded as Diospolis in 293 CE, and rebuilt as Diampolis/Dbilin in the Middle Ages.

b_philippopolis.first_mention_attestation: Conquered and renamed Philippopolis (Φιλιππόπολις) by Philip II of Macedon in 342 BCE.
b_philippopolis.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Φιλιππόπολις (Philippopolis, 'City of Philip'), named by Philip II of Macedon in 342 BCE; Thracian Pulpudeva yielded the Slavic/modern name Plovdiv.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ammianus Marcellinus (Eumolpias) and Jordanes (Pulpudeva) referencing the pre-342 BCE Thracian settlement
older_name_by_867.notes: Pulpudeva (Thracian -deva 'city') either predated or translated Philippopolis and evolved into Slavic Plovdiv.

b_tsepina.first_mention_attestation: Seized by the Byzantine Empire in the 11th century CE and later liberated by Kaloyan (becoming the capital of Despot Alexius Slav in 1207 CE); no pre-867 CE attestation exists.
b_tsepina.etymology_analysis: Medieval Bulgarian fortress (Greek Τσέπαινα / Tzepaina) in the Chepino Valley, likely linked to Slavic *cěpiti ('to split/cleave'), referring to the steep rocky crag.

b_stanimaka.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Thracians/Greek colonists as Stenimachos (Στενήμαχος) around 400–300 BCE.
b_stanimaka.etymology_analysis: Stanimaka is the Slavicized form of Ancient Greek Στενήμαχος (Stenímachos, 'narrow pass/battle'); renamed Asenovgrad in 1934 after Tsar Ivan Asen II (1230 CE). (Renamed Asenovgrad in 1934 CE after Tsar Ivan Asen II.)

b_krichim.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Byzantine sources c. 1198–1199 CE as Kritzimos (stronghold of Ivanko near Philippopolis), and in the 1230 CE inscription of Tsar Ivan Asen II.
b_krichim.etymology_analysis: Medieval Bulgarian-Byzantine fortress at the mouth of the Vacha gorge, attested from 1198 CE as Kritzimos / Krichim.

b_nevropkop.first_mention_attestation: Under the name Nevrokop, first mentioned in the Ottoman Tahrir defter of 1444 CE (near the Roman ruins of Nicopolis ad Nestum, founded 105–106 CE).

morphemes.translation: medieval/Ottoman adaptation of Nicopolis (or Greek neurokopi)

b_nevropkop.etymology_analysis: Nevrokop (attested 1444 CE) derives from a medieval/Ottoman corruption of nearby Roman Nicopolis ad Nestum (or Greek Neurokopi); renamed Gotse Delchev in 1951 after the 19th-century revolutionary.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Founded by Emperor Trajan in 105–106 CE to mark his victory over the Dacians
older_name_by_867.notes: Nicopolis ad Nestum flourished in late antiquity (4th–6th centuries CE) before being destroyed/abandoned.

b_kalyatta.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological excavations date the Kalyata fortress near Yakoruda to the 4th–5th centuries CE (with Justinianic coins and 12th–13th century layers), but the modern name Kalyata is an undated Ottoman-era Turkish loanword with no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_kalyatta.etymology_analysis: Bulgarian definite form of dialectal kalya (from Ottoman Turkish kale < Arabic qal'a, 'fortress'), meaning 'the Fortress'.

b_dospat.first_mention_attestation: Probably founded by Despot Alexius Slav in the late 12th or early 13th century CE (c. 1207–1230), from whose title (despot) the town's name derives.

b_kavurskotokale.first_mention_attestation: Ruined medieval fortress along the Devinska River near Devin; its Ottoman-Bulgarian name ('Infidel's Fortress') has no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_kavurskotokale.etymology_analysis: Post-medieval/Ottoman-era Bulgarian-Turkish descriptive name meaning 'the Infidel's (Christian's) Fortress', from Ottoman Turkish gâvur ('non-Muslim') + kale ('fortress').

b_zherkovo.first_mention_attestation: During the Bulgarian Empire (medieval period, 12th–14th centuries), the settlement on the site of modern Kardzhali was known as Zherkovo (a name used until the 17th century); no pre-867 CE written attestation of Zherkovo exists.

b_zherkovo.etymology_analysis: Medieval Bulgarian name for Kardzhali used until the 17th century, before being replaced by Kardzhali (after 18th-century Turkish leader Kırca Ali).

b_lyutitsa.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Byzantine eparchial lists (Leo VI's Notitia Episcopatuum, c. 901–902 CE) as a bishopric near Ivaylovgrad.
b_lyutitsa.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic ljut ('fierce/steep') + suffix -itsa; attested in 9th–10th century Byzantine Notitiae Episcopatuum as an episcopal seat.

b_smolyan.first_mention_attestation: Adopted by official decree in 1934 CE (replacing Ottoman Paşmaklı), named after the 7th-century Slavic tribe Smolyani; modern town formed in 1960 CE by merging Ustovo, Raykovo, and Ezerovo.

b_ustra.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by 13th-century Byzantine chroniclers George Akropolites and Theodore Skoutariotes in accounts of Bulgarian Emperor Michael II Asen's 1254 CE Rhodope campaign; archaeologically built in the 10th century CE.
b_ustra.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortress name in the eastern Rhodope Mountains; linked either to South Slavic/Old Church Slavonic ustro/utro ('dawn, east') or a pre-Slavic Thracian toponym.

b_byalgrad.first_mention_attestation: Archaeologically dated to the 12th century CE (late 12th c. Byzantine/Bulgarian keep near Gugutka); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_byalgrad.etymology_analysis: Bulgarian compound meaning 'White Fortress', referring to the bright color of the limestone blocks used in its construction.

b_szerem.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 4th century BCE as an Illyrian-Celtic settlement; later major Roman city of Sirmium (Strabo, Geographica VII; Pliny the Elder).

b_szerem.etymology_analysis: Ancient Sirmium (conflated in folk etymology with Triballian king Syrmus) evolved into South Slavic Srem and Hungarian Szerém; the modern Serbian name Sremska Mitrovica adds 'of St. Demetrius'.

b_ilok.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as a medieval town in 1267 CE (Hungarian Újlak); Roman frontier fort Cuccium previously stood on the site (1st–2nd century CE).
b_ilok.etymology_analysis: Croatian Ilok is adapted from Hungarian Újlak ('new dwelling / new lodge').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman frontier records (1st–2nd century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Danube limes fortification Cuccium occupied the site prior to medieval Újlak/Ilok.

b_zemun.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Taurunum by Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, 77 CE); Slavic name Zemln/Zemlyn recorded in the 9th century CE (827 CE).
b_zemun.etymology_analysis: Slavic Zemln/Zemun derives from zemlja ('earth') or zemunica ('dugout'), referring to earthen fortifications or loess dwellings; replaced Celtic/Roman Taurunum.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, 77 CE)

b_aytos.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval written chronicles in 1206 CE (destroyed by Crusaders under Henry of Flanders; also Niketas Choniates and Geoffroi de Villehardouin); fortress remains date to 3rd–4th and 13th–14th centuries CE.
b_aytos.etymology_analysis: Derived from Byzantine Greek Aetós (Ἀετός, 'eagle'), referring to the hilltop fortress overlooking the Aytos pass.

b_provadiya.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Byzantine and Bulgarian chronicles in the late 11th century CE under the Byzantine name Provat/Provaton and Bulgarian Ovech; archaeologically active 3rd–7th and 10th–17th centuries CE.
b_provadiya.etymology_analysis: Bulgarian Provadiya derives from Byzantine Greek Provat/Provaton (linked to 'sheep'—translated by Bulgarians as Ovech from ovtsa 'sheep'—or to a narrow pass).

b_ktenia.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1278 CE by Byzantine chronicler George Pachymeres during the Uprising of Ivaylo (captured by Byzantines alongside Lardea); archaeological ruins are Roman/medieval.
b_ktenia.etymology_analysis: Medieval Byzantine Greek fortress name Κτένια (from kténion, diminutive of kteís 'comb', likely describing the indented rock ridge or battlements).

b_preslav.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 893 CE at the Council of Preslav when Boris I moved the Bulgarian capital from Pliska to Preslav; originated as an unfortified 9th-century Slavic settlement.
b_preslav.etymology_analysis: Old Slavonic Preslav literally means 'The Most Glorious'; 'Veliki' ('Great') was added later to distinguish it as the imperial capital.

b_tutrakan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as Tutrakan by 867 CE; preceded by the Roman Danube limes fortress Transmarisca (1st century CE, c. 50 CE), with the medieval Bulgarian settlement emerging after Transmarisca's 7th-century destruction.
b_tutrakan.etymology_analysis: Roman castrum Transmarisca ('across the marsh') was adapted in medieval Bulgarian/Turkish as Tutrakan (Turtucaia).

older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Transmarisca is the direct ancestor of Tutrakan.

b_shumen.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing as Šimeonis in 1153 CE by Arab geographer al-Idrisi; archaeologically fortified from the Iron Age through the 8th–10th centuries CE.
b_shumen.etymology_analysis: Likely derived from Bulgarian shuma ('deciduous forest'), though an alternative hypothesis (Konstantin Jireček) links it to Tsar Simeon the Great (893–927 CE).

b_hrazgrad.first_mention_attestation: Medieval/Ottoman Hrazgrad/Hezargrad attested from the 15th–16th centuries CE; ancient Roman city of Abritus (attested 251 CE, Battle of Abritus) stood in the vicinity.

morphemes.translation: obscure first element (possibly personal name or Hras)

b_hrazgrad.etymology_analysis: Bulgarian compound ending in -grad ('city'); the first element raz-/hraz- is obscure (Ottoman Turkish adapted it as Hezargrad).

b_sborishte.first_mention_attestation: Modern village in Tvarditsa Municipality, Sliven Province (known as Dzhumalii until 1906 CE); no pre-867 written attestation.
b_sborishte.etymology_analysis: Bulgarian sborishte means 'gathering place' (from sbor 'assembly' + locative -ishte), adopted in 1906 to replace Ottoman Dzhumalii.

b_nikopolis.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 629 CE as Nicopolis on the Danube by Byzantine Emperor Heraclius I following his victory over the Sassanid Empire.
b_nikopolis.etymology_analysis: From Byzantine Greek Nikópolis (Νικόπολις, 'City of Victory'), founded by Emperor Heraclius in 629 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Byzantine foundation under Emperor Heraclius (629 CE)

b_pliven.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Pleven first attested in a 1270 CE Hungarian royal charter; Roman road station Storgosia existed nearby in antiquity (1st–3rd century CE).
b_pliven.etymology_analysis: Slavic toponym Pleven (traditionally linked to pleva 'chaff' / plevnya 'barn' or a Slavicized pre-Slavic root).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman road itineraries (1st–3rd century CE)

b_lovech.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in the 11th century CE (1059 CE) in connection with Pecheneg incursions against Byzantium; ancient Thracian Melta and Roman Prezidium preceded it.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Thracian/Roman archaeological and road records (4th–3rd c. BCE / Roman era)

b_samundzhievo.first_mention_attestation: First recorded as the Ottoman village Samundzhievo in 16th-century Ottoman tax registers; elevated to town status as Orhanie in 1865–1866 and renamed Botevgrad in 1934 CE.

b_sredets.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Serdica in a 1st-century BCE Athenian inscription; renamed Sredets after Khan Krum's 809 CE conquest and Sofia in the 14th century CE.

b_meldi.first_mention_attestation: Attested as mansio Meldia in the Itinerarium Burdigalense (333 CE) and on the Tabula Peutingeriana on the Via Militaris northwest of Serdica.

b_pernik.first_mention_attestation: Although excavated 9th-century fortifications exist, Pernik enters written sources in the late 10th–11th century CE (e.g., John Skylitzes on Emperor Basil II's 1004 and 1016 CE sieges).

b_stipon.first_mention_attestation: Roman defensive station Stipon guarding the Succi (Gate of Trajan) mountain pass on the Via Militaris (Roman imperial period); renamed Ihtiman under Ottoman rule.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman imperial road records (near Succi / Gate of Trajan)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman/Byzantine Stipon preceded Ottoman-era Ihtiman.

b_rila.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in Tsar Ivan Shishman's 1378 CE Rila Charter (as Driska) and as İrlie in 1576 Ottoman registers; ancient Thracian-Roman predecessors Sportela and Roligera stood on the site.

older_name_by_867.notes: Antiquity settlements Sportela and Roligera occupied the site of modern Rila.

b_turnovo.first_mention_attestation: Rose to historical prominence as Tarnovgrad during the 1185 CE Uprising of Asen and Peter; earlier First Bulgarian and Byzantine fortifications existed on Tsarevets hill without pre-867 attestation of the name Tarnovo.

b_cherven.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 11th century CE in an Old Bulgarian apocryphal chronicle; archaeologically a 6th-century Byzantine fortress existed on the site.
b_cherven.etymology_analysis: Bulgarian cherven ('red'), referring to the reddish limestone cliffs and soil of the Cherni Lom river bend.

b_elena.first_mention_attestation: Attested since 1430 CE as Stramena and Eliana (founded before the 15th century CE).

b_gabrovo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1477 CE as Gabruva in Ottoman records; modern form Gabrovo appears in the 17th century CE.
b_gabrovo.etymology_analysis: From Slavic gabar ('hornbeam') + -ovo, referring to hornbeam trees at the settlement site.

b_vratsa.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Slavic Vratsa (Vratitsa) is attested in 14th-century Bulgarian sources (e.g., Gospel of Vratsa) and Ottoman registers; preceded by the Roman fortress Valve ('double door', c. 150 CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman imperial period (Valve at Vratsata pass)

b_lom.first_mention_attestation: Ottoman/modern Lom Palanka is first mentioned in 1704 CE; preceded on the same site by the Roman frontier fortress Almus (c. 150 CE) on the Almus (Lom) River.
b_lom.etymology_analysis: Named after the Lom River (Latin Almus), a right tributary of the Danube.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Danubian limes records
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Almus evolved phonetically into Slavic Lom.

b_orehovo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a Hungarian charter of 1283 CE, and in 1396 CE during the Crusade of Nicopolis (as Rahova/Oreov); nearby 9th-century fortress Kamaka is archaeologically dated.
b_orehovo.etymology_analysis: Derived from Bulgarian oreh ('walnut') + -ovo (adapted in Ottoman Turkish as Rahova).

b_kutlovitsa.first_mention_attestation: Slavic Kutlovitsa (Ottoman Kutlofça) is documented in late 16th-century Ottoman defters (c. 1575 CE) and 1688 CE; preceded by Roman Castra ad Montanesium / Civitas Montanensium (c. 150–160 CE).
b_kutlovitsa.etymology_analysis: Medieval Slavic Kutlovitsa derives from a word for a valley/basin; renamed Ferdinand in 1890 and Montana in 1993 after Roman Montanesium.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman imperial epigraphy (1st–2nd century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Castra ad Montanesium preceded medieval Kutlovitsa.

b_famagusta.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Arsinoe by Ptolemy II Philadelphus c. 270 BCE (described by Strabo in the 1st century BCE); Greek name Ammochostos recorded from the 4th century CE.

b_nicosia.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Lidir (Ledra) on the 672 BCE Neo-Assyrian Prism of Esarhaddon; Byzantine Leucosia/Lefkosia attested in late antiquity and the Byzantine era.

b_limisol.first_mention_attestation: The name Nemesos / Lemesos (Limassol) is first explicitly attested in the 10th century CE (Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, De Thematibus); preceded by ancient Neapolis / Theodosiana (451 CE).

older_name_by_867.notes: Early Christian Neapolis/Theodosiana and Greek Nemesos evolved into Lemesos/Limassol.

b_paphos.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in Homer's Odyssey (viii.362, c. 700 BCE) and on the Neo-Assyrian Prism of Esarhaddon (673–672 BCE).
b_paphos.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek / Eteocypriot city name Páphos, celebrated in Greek tradition as the cult center of Aphrodite.

b_iraklio.first_mention_attestation: Ancient port of Knossos attested as Heracleium by Strabo (Geographica, late 1st century BCE); refounded in 824 CE by Andalusian Arabs as rabḍ al-ḫandaq (Hellenized as Chandax).

b_agiosnikolaos.first_mention_attestation: The settlement name (Venetian Porto di San Nicolò → Greek Agios Nikolaos) arose in the Venetian period (after 1204 CE); preceded by ancient Lato pros Kamara (Kamara, c. 150 CE).

older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Hierapytna evolved directly into Ierapetra.

b_chania.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Mycenaean Linear B tablets from Knossos as Ku-do-ni-ja (c. 1400 BCE) and as Kydonia in Homer's Odyssey; Arab/Byzantine name al-Khan / Chania emerged in the 9th–10th centuries CE.

b_rethymno.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Rhithymna on Classical/Hellenistic coinage (4th–3rd century BCE) and later by Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy.

b_ankyra.first_mention_attestation: Attested during Alexander the Great's campaign in 333 BCE (Arrian); possibly identical with Hittite Ankuwaš (2nd millennium BCE).

b_attalia.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Pergamene garrison by Eumenes I (r. 263–241 BCE) and named Attaleia (Ἀττάλεια) after his grandfather Attalus.
b_attalia.etymology_analysis: Named Attáleia (Ἀττάλεια) after the Attalid dynasty of Pergamon (Attalus).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical tradition prior to Pergamene refoundation
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally named Agroeira or Alloeira before becoming Attalea.

b_synaos.first_mention_attestation: Attested as a Phrygian/Lydian city and bishopric from Late Antiquity (Synaus, Συναός, suffragan of Laodicea in Phrygia; Roman/Byzantine castle and Notitiae Episcopatuum).
b_synaos.etymology_analysis: Pre-Turkish Anatolian toponym Synaós / Synaus (Συναός), which evolved phonetically into modern Turkish Simav.

b_tabala.first_mention_attestation: Attested on Roman provincial coinage (1st–2nd century CE, e.g., under Antoninus Pius / Faustina II), in Hierocles' Synecdemus (c. 535 CE, as Gabala/Tabala), and at the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE).

morphemes.translation: Lydian town on the Hermus River; possibly related to Anatolian/Luwian *Tapāla

b_tabala.etymology_analysis: Greek Τάβαλα (Tábala), a Roman and Byzantine town and bishopric on the Hermus River in Lydia; possibly of pre-Greek Anatolian/Luwian origin (cf. Hittite mountain name Tapāla).

b_ablastha.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ablasta (Armenian: Աբլաստա) by Armenian historians in the early 11th century CE, following mid-10th-century Armenian settlement; preceded in antiquity by Plasta / Plastentia (Greek: Πλαστεντία).

morphemes.translation: early medieval adaptation of ancient Plasta/Plastentia; later folk-etymologized via Arabic al-bustān ('the orchard')

b_ablastha.etymology_analysis: Medieval Armenian Ablasta (later Ablistan, Albistan, modern Turkish Elbistan) continues or adapts the ancient name Plasta/Plastentia, later reinterpreted via Arabic al-bustān ('the orchard').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman/late antique Plasta / Plastentia (Πλαστεντία), attested on regional Roman milestones (c. 3rd–4th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Plasta and Plastentia (Πλαστεντία) in antiquity before the mid-10th-century CE settlement named Ablasta.

b_dalanda.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE) as Daranda/Dalanda in Cappadocia; later recorded in Byzantine sources as Taranta.
b_dalanda.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek Anatolian toponym featuring the -nda suffix (cf. Luwian/Cappadocian place names), preserved through Classical Daranda/Dalanda and Byzantine Taranta to modern Turkish Darende.

b_osdara.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Roman Itinerarium Antonini (Antonine Itinerary, late 3rd / early 4th century CE) as a road station between Arabissus/Cappadocia and Melitene.

morphemes.translation: Roman road-station toponym in eastern Cappadocia

b_osdara.etymology_analysis: Latinized form of an indigenous Cappadocian/Anatolian toponym recorded in the Antonine Itinerary along the military road to Melitene.

b_karnalis.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Roman Itinerarium Antonini (Antonine Itinerary, c. 300 CE) as a road station in Cappadocia.
b_karnalis.etymology_analysis: Latinized Cappadocian/Anatolian place name attested in the Roman road network of eastern Anatolia; the county name Azysia in the repo reflects the nearby district/station.

b_euspena.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Roman Itinerarium Antonini (c. 300 CE; Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire dates Euspena at Kangal to 30 BCE–640 CE).

morphemes.translation: Roman-era settlement name at modern Kangal

b_euspena.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Cappadocian/Anatolian toponym preserved in Latinized form as Euspena in Roman road itineraries.

b_gauraina.first_mention_attestation: Attested under the name Gauraina in Classical Antiquity (4th century BCE / Achaemenid–Hellenistic Cappadocia); the site is also identified with Iron Age Tilgarimmu (9th century BCE) and Bronze Age Tegarama (c. 1344 BCE).
b_gauraina.etymology_analysis: Classical Greek/Cappadocian Gauraina, surviving through Armenian Gurin/Kiwrin into modern Turkish Gürün.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Neo-Assyrian annals of Shalmaneser III (859–824 BCE) for Tilgarimmu; Hittite records of Šuppiluliuma I (c. 1344–1322 BCE) for Tegarama
older_name_by_867.notes: Scholars identify Gürün with Iron Age Tilgarimmu and Late Bronze Age Tegarama.

b_tanadaris.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Roman Itinerarium Antonini (c. 300 CE) as Tanadaris, located at modern Tanır in Afşin/Kahramanmaraş.

morphemes.translation: ancient settlement name preserved in modern Turkish Tanır

b_tanadaris.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Anatolian/Cataonian toponym recorded in Latinized form as Tanadaris in Roman itineraries, surviving as modern Tanır.

b_dasmenda.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Strabo in Geographica (1st century BCE) as Dasmenda (Ancient Greek: Δασμένδα), a stronghold with a sheer ascent in Cappadocia.
b_dasmenda.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek Anatolian/Cappadocian toponym cited by Paul Kretschmer as a classic example of the Anatolian -nd- place-name element.

b_sebasteia.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sebasteia (Greek: Σεβάστεια) in Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE), the Antonine Itinerary (c. 200 CE), and early Christian ecclesiastical histories; earlier mentioned by Pliny the Elder and Strabo as Megalopolis/Sebaste.
b_sebasteia.etymology_analysis: Named Sebasteia in honor of Emperor Augustus (Greek Sebastós); modern Turkish Sivas derives from Greek Sebasteia / Armenian Sebastia.

b_sebastopolis.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sebastopolis (Greek: Σεβαστούπολις) in Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and the Antonine Itinerary; also known as Heracleopolis (Ἡρακλειούπολις) and site of the 692 CE Battle of Sebastopolis.
b_sebastopolis.etymology_analysis: Greek Sebastoupolis ('city of Augustus'), also called Heracleopolis ('city of Heracles'); modern Turkish Sulusaray ('watery palace').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical/Roman sources (Sulusaray Wikipedia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Also known in antiquity as Heracleopolis (Ἡρακλειούπολις).

b_pedachtoe.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Martyrdom of Saint Athenogenes of Pedachtoë (martyred 303 CE; hagiography composed 4th–6th century CE) and as an archbishopric of Armenia Prima.

morphemes.translation: toponym of Pontus/Armenia Prima, later Ottoman Bedohtun

b_pedachtoe.etymology_analysis: Ancient Pontic/Cappadocian toponym Pedachtoë (also known as Heracleopolis), preserved in Ottoman records as Bedohtun (modern Güneykaya, Yıldızeli).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ecclesiastical lists / Pedachtoë Wikipedia
older_name_by_867.notes: Also known as Heracleopolis (Ἡρακλειούπολις) in ecclesiastical records.

b_malandra.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Malandara in Roman/Late Antique Cappadocian itineraries (Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire dates Malandara at Şarkışla to 30 BCE–640 CE).
b_malandra.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Anatolian/Cappadocian place name recorded in Latinized form as Malandara in the vicinity of Sebasteia.

b_ribnicapodgorica.first_mention_attestation: The medieval Slavic settlement Ribnica and name Podgorica are first attested in 1326 CE in the Kotor archives; current_repo_state uses county-seat fallback Dioklêe (Doclea, c. 150 CE), which is recorded in older_name_by_867.

morphemes.translation: city of the Illyrian Dokleatai tribe

b_ribnicapodgorica.etymology_analysis: Repo name Dioklêe reflects ancient Doclea (Illyrian tribe Dokleatai); Ribnica derives from the Ribnica River (from Slavic riba, 'fish'); Podgorica means 'under the little hill (Gorica)'.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Claudius Ptolemy, Geography (2nd century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Doclea (Diokleia) was the Roman/Illyrian city near Podgorica, alongside Roman Birziminium.

b_plav.first_mention_attestation: The Plav–Gusinje region on the upper Lim is first attested in historical records in the 1330 CE Dečani chrysobulls (mentioning Hotina Gora); Plav itself is mentioned in medieval Serbian sources from the 13th–14th centuries.
b_plav.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic plav, meaning 'a flooded place' or 'floodplain', referring to the glacial Lake Plav and Lim River basin.

b_drivast.first_mention_attestation: First documented as an episcopal see (Drivastum) in 877 CE at the Council of Dumno (concilium Delmitanum), and attested archaeologically and in chronicles by the late 10th century.

morphemes.translation: ancient/medieval town name, yielding Albanian Drisht

b_drivast.etymology_analysis: From Latin Drivastum (with accentual shift Drísht < Drívastum via an Adriatic Illyrian intermediary), Serbian Drivost, Italian Drivasto.

b_danj.first_mention_attestation: Attested as a župa/town of the Kingdom of Duklja under Constantine Bodin (1081–1116 CE) and in the Ragusan–Serbian peace treaty signed at Dagnum on 25 March 1326 CE.

morphemes.translation: medieval fortress and river-crossing town on the Drin

b_danj.etymology_analysis: Medieval Latin Dagnum (Serbian Danj, Albanian Danjë/Dejë, Italian Dagno), a strategic fortress and customs point near modern Vau i Dejës.

b_skadar.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Skodra / Scodra by the Illyrian tribe of the Labeatae in the 4th century BCE; annexed by Rome in 168 BCE after the Third Illyrian War.

morphemes.translation: capital of the Illyrian Labeatae and Ardiaei

b_skadar.etymology_analysis: From Illyrian/Latin Scodra, yielding Albanian Shkodër/Shkodra, South Slavic Skadar, Italian Scutari, and Ottoman Turkish İşkodra.

b_moraca.first_mention_attestation: The Morača Monastery was founded in 1252 CE by Stefan Vukanović Nemanjić in the Morača River valley.

morphemes.translation: river and valley name in central Montenegro

b_moraca.etymology_analysis: Named after the Morača River (a major tributary of Lake Skadar), where the 1252 CE Morača Monastery was built.

b_antivari.first_mention_attestation: The name Antibarium is first quoted in the 10th century CE (Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus / Byzantine sources); a 6th-century castle Antipargal is only conjecturally identified with Bar.

morphemes.translation: Bari (city across the Adriatic in Italy)

b_antivari.etymology_analysis: From Latin Antibarium / Greek Antivarion ('opposite Bari', referring to its position across the Adriatic Sea from Bari, Italy), shortened in South Slavic to Bar.

b_ulcinj.first_mention_attestation: Foundation in the 5th century BCE by Colchians is mentioned in the 3rd-century BCE poem of Apollonius of Rhodes; attested historically in Livy (45.26.2) for 168 BCE as Olcinium.
b_ulcinj.etymology_analysis: From Illyrian/Latin Olcinium (also Ulcinium), yielding Serbian/Montenegrin Ulcinj, Albanian Ulqin, and Italian Dulcigno.

b_cattaro.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 168 BCE as Acruvium / Ascrivium (Greek: Ἀσκρήβιον) in Roman Dalmatia; later recorded in Byzantine sources as Dekatera (Δεκάτερα).

morphemes.translation: ancient and Byzantine names of Kotor

b_cattaro.etymology_analysis: Ancient Acruvium/Ascrivium was succeeded by Byzantine Greek Dekatera (Medieval Latin Cattarum, Italian Cattaro, Slavic Kotor).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman sources (168 BCE, Kotor Wikipedia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Acruvium/Ascrivium in Roman times before Byzantine Dekatera / Cattaro / Kotor.

b_trebinje.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 10th century CE in Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus's De Administrando Imperio as Terbounia (Τερβουνία) / Travunia.

morphemes.translation: early medieval principality and town in eastern Herzegovina

b_trebinje.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Terbounia in 10th-century Byzantine Greek (Latin Travunia/Tribunia, South Slavic Trebinje).

b_onogost.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the Ostrogothic fortress Anagastum after 459 CE (built on the 4th-century CE Roman castrum Anderba, itself on an Illyrian settlement); Slavicized as Onogošt in the Middle Ages.

morphemes.translation: Ostrogothic fortress name (possibly from Gothic personal name Anagast)

b_onogost.etymology_analysis: From Late Latin/Ostrogothic Anagastum, Slavicized as Onogošt; renamed Nikšić in the mid-15th century after the Nikšići tribe.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman/Late Antique sources (Nikšić Wikipedia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman castrum Anderba (4th century CE) preceded Ostrogothic Anagastum (after 459 CE).

b_risan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Illyrian Rhizon (Greek: Ῥίζων), capital of the Ardiaean Kingdom and last stronghold of Queen Teuta during the First Illyrian War (229–228 BCE); Roman Rhizinium/Risinium.

morphemes.translation: oldest settlement in the Bay of Kotor

b_risan.etymology_analysis: From ancient Illyrian Rhizon (Roman Rhizinium/Risinium), surviving into South Slavic Risan and Italian Risano.

b_beograd.first_mention_attestation: The Slavic name Beograd is first recorded on 16 April 878 CE in a letter from Pope John VIII to Boris I of Bulgaria; preceded by Celtic/Roman Singidunum (3rd century BCE / 75 BCE).
b_beograd.etymology_analysis: South Slavic Beograd ('White City/Fortress'), calqued in the repo as Old High German Wîtzburch ('white fortress').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical/Roman sources (Singidunum Wikipedia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Celtic Scordisci settlement (3rd century BCE) and Roman legionary fortress Singidunum (conquered 75 BCE), destroyed in the 7th century CE.

b_smederevo.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Charter of Byzantine Emperor Basil II in 1019 CE (under the Eparchy of Braničevo); preceded in Roman times by Vinceia (1st century BCE).

morphemes.translation: possibly from Saint Demetrius (Skok), personal name Smender, or smet ('deep snow') + drevo ('wood')

b_smederevo.etymology_analysis: Attested from 1019 CE; Petar Skok derives it from Saint Demetrius, while other hypotheses link it to personal name Smender or Old Serbian smet + drevo.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Moesia Superior sources (Smederevo Wikipedia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman settlement Vinceia existed at or near the site from the 1st century BCE.

b_rudnik.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Rudnik is recorded in 1293 CE (though archaeological evidence shows Roman and Bronze Age mining on the mountain).
b_rudnik.etymology_analysis: Serbian rudnik literally means 'mine', referring to Mount Rudnik's rich silver, lead, and copper deposits.

b_kragujevac.first_mention_attestation: First written mention in an Ottoman cadastral survey (defter) of 1476 CE as 'Kraguyfoça' in the Sanjak of Smederevo.
b_kragujevac.etymology_analysis: Derived from Serbian kraguj ('cinereous vulture', a hunting bird common in the medieval forests of the area).

b_macva.first_mention_attestation: The town and banate of Mačva (Macsó) is first attested in the mid-13th century CE (Rostislav Mikhailovich styled Dominus de Macho from 1254 CE); current_repo_state uses county-seat fallback Sîrmjen (Sirmium, 4th century BCE).
b_macva.etymology_analysis: Repo name Sîrmjen adapts ancient Sirmium (modern Sremska Mitrovica), which gave its name to the region of Syrmia (Srem) and the 11th-century Byzantine Theme of Sirmium.

current_repo_state.name: Sîrmjen
current_repo_state.b_origin: Sîrmjen — Historical Option A seat of c_macva

b_debrc.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1282 CE as the first capital of the Realm of Stefan Dragutin (Lower Syrmia / Mačva).

morphemes.translation: settlement on the Sava River (cf. Slavic *dъbrь, 'ravine, valley')

b_debrc.etymology_analysis: Medieval Serbian settlement on the Sava between Belgrade and Šabac, serving as Stefan Dragutin's royal seat from 1282 CE.

b_krupanj.first_mention_attestation: First written mention in 1417 CE as Crupagn, a medieval silver mining settlement.

morphemes.translation: large, coarse (or personal name / mining term)

b_krupanj.etymology_analysis: Medieval Serbian mining town first attested in 1417 CE as Crupagn in Dubrovnik/regional records.

b_uzice.first_mention_attestation: First historical record mentioning Užice by name dates to 1329 CE (as a fortress under the Vojinović family during Stefan Dušan's reign); Roman municipium Capedunum existed in the area.

morphemes.translation: medieval Serbian fortress and town name

b_uzice.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1329 CE; the surrounding area previously hosted the Roman/Celtic municipium of Capedunum.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Dalmatia sources (Užice Wikipedia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman municipium of Capedunum (with Celtic -dun 'fortress') existed in the Užice area in Roman times.

b_pristina.first_mention_attestation: Pristina is first recorded in 1342 CE as a village during the reign of Stefan Dušan; repo name Chwosne (Hvosno) is first mentioned in 1201–1208 CE in the Life of Saint Simeon.
b_pristina.etymology_analysis: Priština is attested from 1342 CE; the county/repo name Hvosno (Chwosne) derives from Old Slavic hvost ('thick wood') and is attested from 1201–1208 CE.

b_prizren.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1019 CE under Byzantine Emperor Basil II in the form Prisdriana; the fortress likely appears in Procopius (6th century CE) as Petrizen, and the city is traditionally linked to Roman Theranda.

morphemes.translation: city and bishopric name attested from 1019 CE

b_prizren.etymology_analysis: Attested as Prisdriana in 1019 CE (possibly continuing late antique Petrizen / Roman Theranda).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Procopius, De Aedificiis (6th century CE) for Petrizen; Roman Dardania for Theranda
older_name_by_867.notes: Prizren fortress is likely Procopius's Petrizen (6th c. CE), and the town is traditionally associated with Roman Theranda.

b_pec.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Peć (Ždrelnik) is attested from the late 12th century (annexed by Stefan Nemanja 1180–1190 CE); built on or near Roman Siparantum (Ptolemy, 2nd century CE) / Pescium.

morphemes.translation: cave, furnace (referring to caves in the Rugova Canyon)

b_pec.etymology_analysis: Serbian Peć means 'cave' (archaic) or 'furnace', referring to the caves in the nearby Rugova Canyon; Albanian Peja derives via Ottoman İpek.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Claudius Ptolemy, Geography (2nd century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Medieval city was possibly built on the ruins of Roman municipium Siparantum (Pescium).

b_zvecan.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1093 CE as a border fortress of Serbian Grand Župan Vukan during the Byzantine–Serbian War (1090–1095).

morphemes.translation: medieval fortress on a volcanic cone above the Ibar River

b_zvecan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Serbian fortress first attested in 1093 CE in accounts of Grand Župan Vukan's wars with Emperor Alexios I Komnenos.

b_podujevo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical records in the 1455 CE Ottoman cadastral survey (defter); Roman Vendenisi existed nearby at Gllamnik.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Llap region

b_podujevo.etymology_analysis: Slavic toponym attested from the 1455 CE Ottoman defter; Albanian Besianë is a modern renaming.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tabula Peutingeriana / Roman Dardania itineraries (Vendenisi, 4th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman settlement Vendenisi was located at nearby Gllamnik.

b_hotca.first_mention_attestation: First written traces of the town date to 1336 CE, when it was known as Hotča or Hoča.

morphemes.translation: medieval trading town on the Drina, later Foča

b_hotca.etymology_analysis: Medieval Hotča/Hoča (first attested 1336 CE), evolving phonetically into Ottoman and modern Foča.

b_prijepolje.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned for the first time in writing by Guillaume Adam (Gijom Adam) in 1332 CE.
b_prijepolje.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic prije ('before') + polje ('field'), referring to the settlement reached by caravans just before the plains of Ivanje and Velika Župa.

b_breznica.first_mention_attestation: The medieval town of Breznica (modern Pljevlja), named after the Breznica River, has its first documentary attestation in the 14th century CE (1338 CE); preceded by Roman Municipium S at Komini (1st–4th centuries CE).
b_breznica.etymology_analysis: Named after the Breznica River (from Slavic breza, 'birch'); from the 14th century CE it bore the double name Breznik and Pljevlja.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Dalmatia epigraphy at Komini (Pljevlja Wikipedia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman city Municipium S (Komini) flourished in the 1st–4th centuries CE.

b_brskovo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned between 1219 and 1228 CE in a trade charter, and in the Ston charter (1253 CE) of King Stefan Uroš I.

morphemes.translation: medieval mining town and mint (Latin Brescia)

b_brskovo.etymology_analysis: Medieval Serbian silver-mining town near Mojkovac (Latinized as Brescia in Ragusan/Venetian sources), first attested 1219–1228 CE.

b_visegrad.first_mention_attestation: The settlement of Višegrad was first mentioned in 1407 CE (and more frequently after 1427 CE in Ragusan caravan records).
b_visegrad.etymology_analysis: South Slavic Višegrad ('upper town' or 'high fortress'), first attested in 1407 CE.

b_gorazde.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1379 CE as a trading settlement on the Drina River, and in 1444 CE as a fortress.

morphemes.translation: capable, skilled, clever (or personal name Gorazd)

b_gorazde.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Slavonic word/personal name gorazd ('capable, skilled'), first attested as a trading settlement in 1379 CE.

b_novotrgoviste.first_mention_attestation: English CK3 localisation renders b_novotrgoviste as 'Stari Trgovište'; medieval Trgovište is attested in the 1455 Ottoman cadastral defter before Novi Pazar ('New Market') was founded nearby (1461–1475 CE). current_repo_state uses county-seat fallback Raschke (Stari Ras / Arsa, c. 554 CE in Procopius), recorded in older_name_by_867.

morphemes.translation: early medieval fortress and capital of Raška

b_novotrgoviste.etymology_analysis: Repo name Raschke reflects medieval Raška / Stari Ras (6th-century Byzantine Arsa); barony key b_novotrgoviste (English CK3 loc: 'Stari Trgovište') refers to 15th-century Trgovište ('marketplace').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Procopius, De Aedificiis (6th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Stari Ras was built on 6th-century Byzantine foundations identified with Procopius's Arsa.

b_budlimlje.first_mention_attestation: The župa of Budimlja is attested from 1213 CE (completion of Đurđevi Stupovi Monastery) and 1219 CE (establishment of the Eparchy of Budimlja by Saint Sava).

morphemes.translation: medieval Serbian župa and village near Berane

b_budlimlje.etymology_analysis: Medieval Slavic toponym in the upper Lim valley (modern village of Budimlja near Berane), attested from the early 13th century CE.

b_zica.first_mention_attestation: The Žiča Monastery was built between 1206 and 1217 CE by King Stefan the First-Crowned and Saint Sava, becoming the seat of the Serbian Archbishopric in 1219 CE.

morphemes.translation: early 13th-century Serbian Orthodox monastery near Kraljevo

b_zica.etymology_analysis: Early 13th-century Serbian monastery and coronation church (founded c. 1206–1217 CE).

b_gradac.first_mention_attestation: The Gradac Monastery was built between 1277 and 1282 CE as an endowment of Queen Helen of Anjou during the reign of Stefan Dragutin.
b_gradac.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic gradac ('little fort/town'), referring to the monastery and plateau above the Gradačka River built 1277–1282 CE.

b_krusevac.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1371 CE as a fortified town and capital by Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović (first charter mention 1387 CE); repo Option A seat Rûdnik (Rudnik) is first attested in 1293 CE.
b_krusevac.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1371 CE by Prince Lazar; traditionally derived from krušac ('river stone'). Repo's Option A seat Rûdnik (1293 CE) is also post-867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Rûdnik
current_repo_state.b_origin: Rûdnik — Historical Option A seat of c_sumadija

b_koznik.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a decree of Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović (r. 1371–1389 CE), and later in 1405 CE decrees of Despot Stefan Lazarević.
b_koznik.etymology_analysis: Highland fortified castle above the Rasina River, first attested in the late 14th century CE under Prince Lazar.

b_prokuplje.first_mention_attestation: First attested under the name Prokuplje ('Fortress of St. Procopios') in 1395 CE; earlier Roman and Early Byzantine settlements on the site were known as Hammeum and Komplos.
b_prokuplje.etymology_analysis: Derived from the name of Saint Procopius of Scythopolis (d. 303 CE), whose relics were translated to the town's church in the late 14th century, yielding 'Prokuplje' (place of St. Procopius).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Via Militaris road station Hammeum (1st–4th century CE) and 6th-century CE Early Byzantine Komplos
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Hammeum stood on the Via Militaris; by the 6th century CE the settlement was known as Komplos.

b_sjenica.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1253 CE as a customs stop on the trade road to Dubrovnik (Ragusa).
b_sjenica.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *sěnica ('hayloft' or 'hay-meadow', derived from *sěno 'hay'), reflecting the pastoral plateau of the Pešter-Sjenica basin. The repository currently uses the fictionalized name 'Goltwalt'.

b_arilje.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1219 CE when Saint Sava proclaimed the monastery at Arilje the seat of the Moravica episcopate.

morphemes.translation: Saint Achillius of Larissa (4th century CE)

b_arilje.etymology_analysis: Derived from Saint Achillius (Ahilije -> Arilje), the 4th-century CE bishop of Larissa whose relics were brought to the site by refugees after the 10th century CE.

b_rujno.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 1537 CE in the colophon of the Rujno Four Gospels printed at Rujno Monastery (established in the 15th century CE in Rujno župa).
b_rujno.etymology_analysis: Named after the 'ruj' (sumac / smoke tree) plant abundant in the Đetinja river valley, giving its name to both the medieval župa of Rujno and Rujno Monastery.

b_branicevo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 879 CE as a bishopric (Eparchy of Braničevo) in ecclesiastical records; it succeeded the ruined Roman city of Viminacium.

morphemes.translation: to defend / fortified frontier or enclosure

b_branicevo.etymology_analysis: South Slavic toponym from *braniti ('to defend') or *braničь ('defender / border post'), referring to the Danubian frontier defense near the ruins of Viminacium.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman provincial capital of Moesia Superior (1st century CE; capital from 87 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Viminacium was destroyed by Slavs in the 6th century CE; medieval Braničevo arose on/near its ruins.

b_kucevo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in historical records of the Kučevo area by 1428 CE (and as the Hungarian Banate of Kučevo in the late 13th century CE).
b_kucevo.etymology_analysis: Toponym of uncertain origin, with proposals ranging from South Slavic *kučь ('Eurasian bittern') or *kuti ('smith') to an early personal or tribal name.

older_name_by_867.notes: 4th-century CE Roman metallurgical remains exist at Kraku Lu Jordan nearby, but no pre-867 written toponym is verified in English sources.

b_ravno.first_mention_attestation: The medieval Slavic settlement of Ravno is attested in 11th–12th century CE Byzantine and Crusader sources (archaeological phase 9th–12th century CE), succeeding Roman Horreum Margi.
b_ravno.etymology_analysis: South Slavic *ravno ('flat/level [plain]'), describing the Morava valley floodplain; later replaced in the Ottoman era by Ćuprija (from Turkish köprü, 'bridge').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman fort and town of Horreum Margi ('Granary of the Margus', 1st–4th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Important Roman fort on the Via Militaris at the Margus (Great Morava) river.

b_vidin.first_mention_attestation: Attested as medieval Bulgarian Bdin/Vidin by the 10th–11th century CE (besieged by Basil II in 1003 CE); preceded by Celtic Dunonia and Roman Bononia.
b_vidin.etymology_analysis: Slavic/Bulgarian phonological evolution (Bdin -> Vidin) from the Roman name Bononia, itself built on the Celtic settlement Dunonia ('high/fortified place').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Celtic Dunonia and 1st-century CE Roman fort Bononia on the Danubian Limes
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Bononia (1st century CE) directly underlies medieval Bdin/Vidin.

b_kladovo.first_mention_attestation: First recorded under the name Kladovo in 1596 CE in an Austrian military document.
b_kladovo.etymology_analysis: Usually derived from Slavic *klada ('log, tree stump') or *kladenac ('well, spring'), though alternative hypotheses link it to 9th-century Duke Glad or a Celtic root.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman town of Zanes and forts Diana and Pontes (Trajan's Bridge, c. 103–105 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Zanes and the nearby forts Diana and Pontes guarded the Iron Gates Danube crossing.

b_zajecar.first_mention_attestation: Oldest preserved written mention of Zaječar dates to 1466 CE in an Ottoman defter.
b_zajecar.etymology_analysis: From Torlak Serbian *zajec ('hare') + agentive suffix *-ar, meaning 'man who breeds or keeps hares'.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Late Roman imperial palace complex Felix Romuliana (Gamzigrad), built c. 297–311 CE by Emperor Galerius
older_name_by_867.notes: Located c. 11 km west of modern Zaječar.

b_petrus.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the mid-14th century CE when Emperor Stefan Dušan granted the Petrus frontier district (krajište) to župan Vukoslav; the Petruš region appears in Prince Lazar's 1375 CE charter.
b_petrus.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortress name (Serbian Petruš / Petrus) likely from Greek/Latin *petra* ('rock/cliff'), referring to its steep rocky spur above the Crnica river canyon.

b_belogradchik.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned by name in Ottoman tax registers of 1454–1455 CE (though a Roman castrum and medieval Bulgarian fortification existed on the site).
b_belogradchik.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Bulgarian-Ottoman formation meaning 'little white town/fortress', from Slavic *belo* ('white') + *grad* ('town/fort') + Turkish diminutive *-çik.

older_name_by_867.notes: Archaeological evidence of a Roman castrum exists, but no pre-867 written toponym is attested.

b_demetrias.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 294 BCE by Demetrius I Poliorcetes, who synoecized neighboring Magnesian towns; later mentioned by Procopius and Hierocles (6th century CE).
b_demetrias.etymology_analysis: Named after its Hellenistic founder, King Demetrius I Poliorcetes of Macedon (294 BCE).

b_velestino.first_mention_attestation: First attested under the name Velestino in 1208 CE in a letter of Pope Innocent III; built on the site of ancient Pherae.

morphemes.translation: likely from a Slavic personal name or root (e.g. Veles/Velest)

b_velestino.etymology_analysis: Medieval toponym of probable Slavic origin, replacing the ancient Thessalian polis name Pherae.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Homer's Iliad (2.711) and Odyssey (4.798), 8th century BCE
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Thessalian city of Pherae occupied the same site.

b_halmyros.first_mention_attestation: Appears as a middle Byzantine port city (Halmyros) in the late 11th to 12th century CE (post-867 CE resettlement of the Thessalian coast).
b_halmyros.etymology_analysis: From Greek *halmyros* ('salty, brackish'), referring to the brackish coastal waters/marshes near the Pagasetic Gulf.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ancient city of Halos (Classical Greek period, ~10 km south of modern Almyros)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Halos was the Classical-era predecessor in the immediate vicinity.

b_neopatras.first_mention_attestation: First attested under the name Neopatras (Neai Patrai) c. 900 CE in the Notitia Episcopatuum of Emperor Leo VI the Wise; preceded by ancient Hypata.
b_neopatras.etymology_analysis: Medieval Greek *Neai Patrai* ('New Patras'), named by refugees from Patras who resettled the abandoned ancient city of Hypata.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Founded turn of the 5th/4th century BCE as capital of the Aenianes; attested by Procopius (6th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Modern Greek Ypati revives the ancient name Hypata.

b_domokos.first_mention_attestation: Attested under the medieval name Domokos in high medieval Byzantine/Frankish sources (e.g., 13th–14th century CE), succeeding ancient Thaumaci.
b_domokos.etymology_analysis: Medieval Greek phonetic evolution from ancient *Thaumakoi* (said by Livy to be named from the astonishment of travelers suddenly seeing the vast Thessalian plain).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Livy (32.4, copying Polybius) recording Philip V's siege of Thaumaci in 199 BCE

b_gardikia.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the medieval bishopric and fortress of Gardiki / Gardikia in Phthiotis from the 11th century CE (renamed Pelasgia in 1927 CE).
b_gardikia.etymology_analysis: From Slavic *gordikъ / *gradik ('small fortress/town'), Hellenized as Gardiki/Gardikia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical/Early Byzantine ruins of ancient Larisa Kremaste (4th–5th century BCE to early Byzantine period)

b_zetouni.first_mention_attestation: First encountered under the medieval name Zetounion (Zetouni) in the acts of the Fourth Council of Constantinople in 869 CE (two years after 867 CE).

morphemes.translation: medieval name of Lamia (possibly from Slavic *žito 'grain' or pre-Greek)

b_zetouni.etymology_analysis: Medieval Byzantine name *Zetounion* (later Italianized as Zeitoun / Zetouni), which replaced ancient *Lamia* from the late 9th century CE until the 19th century CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ancient Greek city of Lamia (Classical antiquity, 5th–4th century BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Lamia was named after either the mythological Lamia or the Malians.

b_larissa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Classical Greek sources by the 5th century BCE (Peloponnesian War, 431 BCE, as the chief city of Thessaly).
b_larissa.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek ('Pelasgian') toponym understood by ancient lexicographers to mean 'citadel' or 'fortress', also personified in Greek myth as the nymph Larissa.

current_repo_state.name: Larîsse
