b_platamon.first_mention_attestation: The name Platamon emerges for the hill's vicinity in the 10th century CE, with the city and castle first described in the 12th century CE.

morphemes.translation: flat rock by the sea / broad beach

b_platamon.etymology_analysis: From Greek *platamōn* ('flat rock surrounded by the sea' or 'broad coastal ledge'), describing the strategic coastal promontory.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pseudo-Scylax (c. 360 BCE), describing Herakleion as the first Macedonian city beyond the Peneios
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Herakleion occupied the castle hill.

b_servia.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Servia in the mid-10th century CE by Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (though Justinian built the castle in the 6th century CE).
b_servia.etymology_analysis: Derived either from Latin *servo* ('to watch over/guard', translating ancient *Phylacae*) or from the ethnonym *Serb* (Constantine VII's account of early Serbian settlement).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, 1st century CE) and an Ancient Greek inscription from Veroia
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Phylacae (from Greek phylasso, 'to watch over').

b_elasson.first_mention_attestation: The modern form Elassona first appears in the 12th century CE in the writings of Archbishop Eustathius of Thessalonica; earlier known as Oloosson / Lossonos.
b_elasson.etymology_analysis: Medieval Greek phonetic evolution from ancient *Oloosson* (early Byzantine *Lossonos*), with prothetic *e-*.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Homer's Iliad (2.739, 'white Oloosson', 8th century BCE) and Procopius (6th century CE, Lossonos)
older_name_by_867.notes: Chief city of ancient Perrhaebia.

b_trikala.first_mention_attestation: The name Trikala appears in the middle Byzantine period (11th–12th century CE, e.g., Anna Komnene's Alexiad), replacing ancient Trikka / Tricca.

morphemes.translation: evolution of Trikka (or folk-etymologized as 'three good things')

b_trikala.etymology_analysis: Medieval Greek evolution of ancient *Trikka* / *Trikke*, which was mythologically derived from the nymph Trikke, daughter of the river god Peneus.

current_repo_state.name: Trikâle
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Homer's Iliad (8th century BCE), sending 30 ships under Asclepius's sons
older_name_by_867.notes: Site of the oldest Asclepieion in Greece.

b_grevena.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a 10th-century CE Byzantine text (and in 11th-century CE Ohrid ecclesiastical records).
b_grevena.etymology_analysis: Medieval toponym of debated origin, possibly from Latin or Slavic *greben* ('ridge/crest').

b_stagoi.first_mention_attestation: Stagoi is first mentioned in the Diatyposis of Byzantine Emperor Leo VI the Wise (r. 886–912 CE), c. 900 CE.

morphemes.translation: plural toponym (possibly from *eis tous agious* 'to the saints' or *stagon*)

b_stagoi.etymology_analysis: Byzantine ecclesiastical and fortress name *Stagoi* (plural), later replaced in Ottoman times by Turkish *Kalabaka* ('powerful fortress').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Livy (recording Roman campaigns in 197 BCE and 168–167 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Aiginion stood on the same site.

b_pharsalos.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 455 BCE when the Athenian commander Myronides besieged Pharsalos (and on 5th-century BCE coinage).

morphemes.translation: Pharsalos (theonym/toponym of pre-Greek or Thessalian origin)

b_pharsalos.etymology_analysis: Ancient Thessalian city name *Pharsalos* (modern Greek *Farsala*), capital of the Phthian tetrarchy and site of the 48 BCE Battle of Pharsalus.

b_euchaita.first_mention_attestation: First appears in written records in the 4th century CE as the cult center of Saint Theodore Tiron; raised to city status by Emperor Anastasius I (491–518 CE).

morphemes.translation: Hellenized Anatolian toponym (later Ottoman Avhat / Avkat)

b_euchaita.etymology_analysis: Late Roman/Byzantine Pontic city name *Euchaita*, preserved into the Ottoman era as *Avhat* / *Avkat* before being renamed Beyözü.

b_pimolisa.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Strabo (Geographica 12.562, c. 18 CE), who notes Pimolisa was a fortified town on the Halys already destroyed by his time, giving its name to the district Pimolisene.
b_pimolisa.etymology_analysis: Hellenized Anatolian/Paphlagonian toponym *Pimōlisa*, which gave its name to the surrounding district of Pimolisene.

b_pteria.first_mention_attestation: Recorded by Herodotus (Histories 1.75–76) as the city in northern Cappadocia captured by Croesus and site of the Battle of Pteria in 547 BCE.
b_pteria.etymology_analysis: Greek rendering *Pteria* of an Iron Age Anatolian/Phrygian city name, identified archaeologically with the massive site at Kerkenes Dağ.

b_amaseia.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the early Hellenistic period as the first capital of the Kingdom of Pontus (founded 281 BCE) and birthplace of Strabo (64 BCE–24 CE).

morphemes.translation: Amaseia (mythologically linked by Strabo to Amazon queen Amasis)

b_amaseia.etymology_analysis: Ancient Pontic name *Amaseia*, preserved with minimal change through Armenian (Amasia), Ottoman, and modern Turkish (Amasya).

b_gadilon.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Strabo (Geographica 12.547, 553, 560, c. 18 CE) and Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia 6.2), giving its name to the plain of Gadilonitis.

morphemes.translation: town in the fertile plain between the Halys and Amisos

b_gadilon.etymology_analysis: Ancient Pontic toponym *Gadilon* (also *Gazelon*), located near modern Bafra in the Kızılırmak delta.

b_amisos.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Greek colony (Amisos) by Ionians from Miletus/Phocaea in the 6th century BCE (c. 564 BCE) and noted by Hecataeus of Miletus.

morphemes.translation: Amisos (later reinterpreted via *eis Amison* -> Sampsounta -> Samsun)

b_amisos.etymology_analysis: Ancient name *Amisos* (said by Hecataeus to have earlier been called Enete), which evolved through Medieval Greek *eis Amisonta* / *Sampsounta* into Turkish *Samsun*.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hecataeus of Miletus (c. 500 BCE), identifying Amisos with Homeric Enete

b_magnopolis.first_mention_attestation: Completed and renamed Magnopolis by Pompey the Great c. 64–63 BCE (attested in Strabo 12.3.30 and Appian), succeeding Mithridates VI's Eupatoria.
b_magnopolis.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Latin-Greek name ('City of Magnus [Pompey]') given by Pompey the Great when he refounded Mithridates VI's unfinished city of Eupatoria.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Founded by Mithridates VI Eupator (r. 120–63 BCE) at the confluence of the Lycus and Iris
older_name_by_867.notes: Renamed Magnopolis by Pompey after Mithridates' defeat.

b_carissa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ptolemy's Geography (5.4, c. 150 CE) as a town of the Trocmi in Galatia/Pontus.
b_carissa.etymology_analysis: Ancient Anatolian/Galatian toponym *Karissa* (also recorded as *Garsi*) in northern Anatolia.

b_sinope.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Milesian Greek colonists c. 630 BCE and attested in Herodotus and Classical Greek historiography.

morphemes.translation: Sinope (mythologically linked to the nymph Sinope)

b_sinope.etymology_analysis: Ancient Black Sea port name *Sinōpē*, probably of pre-Greek Anatolian origin and later adapted into Turkish as *Sinop*.

b_zagora.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Arrian's Periplus Ponti Euxini (c. 130 CE) and Ptolemy's Geography (5.4) as Zagorus / Zagora on the coast between Sinope and the Halys.

morphemes.translation: coastal town between Sinope and the Halys

b_zagora.etymology_analysis: Ancient Paphlagonian/Pontic coastal toponym *Zagōros* / *Zagōra* (near modern Çayağzı), distinct from the later Slavic toponym Zagora.

b_andrapa.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the bishopric of Andrapa at the Council of Ephesus (431 CE) and Chalcedon (451 CE), returning to its native name after earlier Hellenistic/Roman Neapolis and Neoclaudiopolis.
b_andrapa.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Anatolian toponym *Andrapa* revived in Late Antiquity for the Roman city of Neoclaudiopolis (modern Vezirköprü).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Founded as Neapolis by Pompey (c. 63 BCE) and renamed Neoclaudiopolis under Emperor Claudius (1st century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: In Late Antiquity the city reverted to its original name Andrapa.

b_comana_pontica.first_mention_attestation: Ancient temple-state of Pontus attested from the early Hellenistic period (c. 281 BCE) and described by Strabo (12.3.34), Caesar (Bellum Alexandrinum 34), and Procopius.

morphemes.translation: sacred city of the goddess Ma
of Pontus (to distinguish from Comana in Cappadocia)

b_comana_pontica.etymology_analysis: Hellenized Anatolian name *Komana* (modern Turkish *Gümenek* via medieval *Komada*), qualified as *Pontike* ('Pontic').

b_zela.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Mithridatic Wars (Battle of Zela, 67 BCE), Caesar's victory in 47 BCE ('Veni, vidi, vici'), and Strabo's Geographica.
b_zela.etymology_analysis: Ancient Pontic city name *Zēla*, preserved directly as modern Turkish *Zile*. The repository currently uses the disambiguated name 'Richwarastat'.

b_amastris.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 300 BCE by Queen Amastris (niece of Darius III) through synoecism of Sesamos and neighboring towns; attested by Strabo and in Notitiae Episcopatuum.
b_amastris.etymology_analysis: Named after its Hellenistic founder, the Persian princess Amastris (c. 300 BCE), evolving into modern Turkish *Amasra*.

b_aigialos.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in Homer's Iliad (Book 2, line 855, 8th century BCE) as a coastal town in Paphlagonia, and later by Strabo (12.3.10).
b_aigialos.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek *aigialos* ('seashore, coast-land'), describing its location on the Paphlagonian Black Sea coast.

b_ionopolis.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ionopolis from the 2nd century CE (under Antoninus Pius / Lucius Verus, on coins and in Lucian), renamed from Abonoteichos.
b_ionopolis.etymology_analysis: Greek *Iōnopolis* ('City of Ion / the Ionians'), granted in the 2nd century CE to replace *Abonoteichos*; corrupted into modern Turkish *İnebolu*.

b_paphlagonia.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by Hecataeus of Miletus (c. 500 BCE, FGrH 1 F 198) as Stephanis (Στεφανίς), a town of the Mariandyni, and later by Pseudo-Scylax, Pliny the Elder, Arrian, and Ptolemy as Stephane (Στεφάνη).

b_castamon.first_mention_attestation: Fortified in the 10th century CE by Byzantine commander Manuel Erotikos Komnenos (c. 955–1020 CE) and named Kastra Komnenon ('Castle of the Komnenoi').

b_ziporea.first_mention_attestation: Attested as a town of ancient Paphlagonia inhabited during Roman and Byzantine times (Barrington Atlas / Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire).
b_ziporea.etymology_analysis: Roman- and Byzantine-era Paphlagonian toponym of probable indigenous Anatolian origin, located near modern Karafasıl.

b_kandara.first_mention_attestation: Inhabited from Achaemenid through Roman times and attested by Stephanus of Byzantium (Ethnica, s.v. Kandara) as a town in Paphlagonia three schoeni from Gangra.
b_kandara.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek Anatolian toponym *Kandara*, associated with a temple of Hera Candarene and tentatively located near modern Candere.

b_cerasus.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Xenophon's Anabasis (5.3–5.4, c. 401–400 BCE) as Cerasus (Kerasous), a Sinopean Greek colony on the Black Sea coast.
b_cerasus.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek *Kerasoûs* (whence Latin *Cerasus* and Turkish *Giresun*), traditionally connected either with wild cherries (*kerasos*) or a horn-shaped promontory (*keras*).

b_oinaion.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Arrian's Periplus Ponti Euxini (c. 131 CE) and Greco-Roman geographical sources as Oenoe / Oinaion, a port town of Pontus at the mouth of the Genius river.
b_oinaion.etymology_analysis: Derived from Ancient Greek Oinoē (Οἰνόη) and Byzantine Greek Oinaion (Οἴναιον), likely from oinos ('wine'), which evolved through Turkish Unieh/Unie into modern Ünye.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Arrian, Periplus Ponti Euxini (c. 131 CE); Greco-Roman geographers
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical Greek Oinoē / Latin Oenoe later became Byzantine Greek Oinaion.

b_polemonium.first_mention_attestation: Founded/renamed Polemonium (Πολεμώνιον) in the late 1st century BCE after King Polemon I of Pontus (appointed by Mark Antony c. 36 BCE), attested in Strabo, Pliny, and Arrian.

morphemes.translation: Polemon (personal name of Polemon I of Pontus)

b_polemonium.etymology_analysis: Named Polemōnion (Πολεμώνιον, Latin Polemonium) after King Polemon I of Pontus; the name survives in the nearby Bolaman River, while modern Fatsa derives from Phadisana/Fanizan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica; Fatsa historical records
older_name_by_867.notes: Also known in Greek as Side and Phadisana (from Fanizan, daughter of Pharnaces II of Pontus).

b_koralla.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Arrian's Periplus Ponti Euxini (c. 131 CE, section 13) and the anonymous Periplus as Coralla / Koralla (τὰ Κόραλλα), 100 stadia east of Philocaleia.
b_koralla.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek ta Koralla (τὰ Κόραλλα), a Pontic coastal town on a rocky cape of the same name, which survived in Ottoman/Turkish as Görele.

b_colonea.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 60s BCE by Roman general Gnaeus Pompey as Colonia (Greek Kolōneia / Κολώνεια), later rebuilt by Justinian I (527–565 CE) as a major fortress of Armenia Secunda.
b_colonea.etymology_analysis: From Latin Colonia ('colony'), Hellenized as Kolōneia (Κολώνεια) and Armenianized as Kołonia; later known as Mavrokastron / Karahisar ('Black Fortress') and Şebinkarahisar.

b_neocaesara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Cabeira (Κάβειρα) during the Third Mithridatic War (71 BCE, Plutarch's Life of Lucullus; Strabo Geographica XII.3), refounded as Neocaesarea (Νεοκαισάρεια) c. 64 CE under Nero.
b_neocaesara.etymology_analysis: From Greek Neokaisareia (Νεοκαισάρεια, 'New Caesarea'), honoring the Roman emperor; contracted in Turkish to Niksar.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Plutarch, Life of Lucullus (15.2); Strabo, Geographica (XII.3.30)
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally the Pontic royal fortress of Cabeira, renamed Diospolis by Pompey, Sebaste by Pythodoris, and Neocaesarea c. 64 CE.

b_sinoria.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Strabo's Geographica (Book XII.3.28, c. 23 CE, citing Theophanes of Mytilene) as Sinoria / Synoria (Συνορία), one of Mithridates VI's chief treasure-fortresses near the border of Greater Armenia.
b_sinoria.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Synoria (Συνορία), meaning 'border-land', altered to Sinoria by Theophanes of Mytilene; located near the border between Pontus and Greater Armenia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica XII.3.28
older_name_by_867.notes: Strabo notes the original form Synoria ('border-land') was spelled Sinoria by Theophanes.

b_hypseie.first_mention_attestation: No documented historical settlement named Hypseie is attested in Classical, Roman, or Byzantine sources for Chaldia or Koloneia; appears to be an unattested or corrupted toponym.
b_hypseie.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical sources; possibly a corruption of Greek hypsēlē ('high') or a local microtoponym, but lacking pre-867 CE documentation.

b_nicopolis_ARM.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 63 BCE by Pompey the Great as Nicopolis (Νικόπολις) in Lesser Armenia after his victory over Mithridates VI in the Third Mithridatic War.
b_nicopolis_ARM.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Nikopolis (Νικόπολις, 'Victory City'), founded by Pompey in 63 BCE to commemorate his victory over Mithridates VI of Pontus.

b_satala.first_mention_attestation: Visited by Emperor Trajan in 115 CE, who stationed Legio XV Apollinaris at the castra stativa of Satala; also attested in Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and Procopius.

morphemes.translation: ancient settlement name of uncertain pre-Greek origin

b_satala.etymology_analysis: Ancient Anatolian/Armenian toponym Satala (Σάταλα), attested as a Roman legionary fortress from the early 2nd century CE; evolved into modern Turkish Sadak.

b_kheranion.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval Byzantine/Seljuk sources around the 12th century (e.g., Battle of Şiran, 1120 CE; Pontic Greek Cheriana / Χεροιανά); no confirmed written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kheranion.etymology_analysis: Byzantine Greek Cheroiana / Cheriana (Χεροιανά), rendered in Turkish as Şiran; attested from the Middle/Late Byzantine period.

b_kamisa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Strabo's Geographica (XI.528, XII.560, c. 23 CE) as Camisa / Kamisa (τὰ Κάμισα), an ancient fortress in Lesser Armenia predating Mithridates VI and destroyed in Pompey's campaign (66 BCE).
b_kamisa.etymology_analysis: Pre-Mithridatic Anatolian toponym Hellenized as ta Kamisa (τὰ Κάμισα), giving its name to the district of Camisene; survived into modern times as Kemiş.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica (XI.528, XII.560)
older_name_by_867.notes: Also known as Comassa; refounded as Sebastopolis after c. 3 BCE.

b_tephrice.first_mention_attestation: Founded between 844 and 856 CE (c. 856 CE) by the Paulician leader Karbeas as Tephrike (Τεφρική), capital of the Paulician principality.
b_tephrice.etymology_analysis: Byzantine Greek Tephrikē (Τεφρική), Armenian Tewrik, founded c. 856 CE by Karbeas; adapted into Turkish as Divriği.

b_trebizond.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally founded in 756 BCE by Milesian colonists from Sinope; first contemporaneously attested in Xenophon's Anabasis (c. 400 BCE) as Trapezous (Τραπεζοῦς).

morphemes.translation: table (referring to the flat-topped acropolis plateau)

b_trebizond.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Trapezous (Τραπεζοῦς), derived from trapeza ('table'), referring to the flat-topped tableland promontory of the ancient city; evolved into Trebizond and Turkish Trabzon.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xenophon, Anabasis (IV.8.22, c. 400 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek Trapezous (accusative Trapezounta) is the direct ancestor of Trebizond and Trabzon.

b_rhizus.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Arrian's Periplus of the Euxine Sea (130–131 CE) as a city at the mouth of the Rhizios river (Ῥίζιος ποταμός).
b_rhizus.etymology_analysis: From Greek rhiza ('root / mountain slopes') or Rizaion (Ῥιζαῖον) / Rhizounta, named after the Rhizios river and surrounding mountain slopes; evolved into Turkish Rize.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Arrian, Periplus Ponti Euxini (130–131 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Attested as Rizaion / Rhizios in Greek and Rhizaeum / Rhizus in Latin.

b_hyspiratis.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Strabo's Geographica (XI.14.9, c. 23 CE) as Syspiritis (Συσπιρῖτις) and in Anania Shirakatsi's 7th-century Geography as Sper.
b_hyspiratis.etymology_analysis: From the ancient ethnonym Saspeires (Saspers), recorded as Syspiritis / Hyspiratis in Greek, Sper in Armenian, Speri in Georgian, and İspir in Turkish.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica (XI.14.9); Anania Shirakatsi (7th c. CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Hyspiratis is a variant of Strabo's Syspiritis.

b_baeberdon.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Procopius's De Aedificiis (c. 550s CE) as Baiberdon (Βαϊβερδών), refortified under Justinian I, and in Movses Khorenatsi's History of Armenia as Paypert.
b_baeberdon.etymology_analysis: From medieval Armenian Baydberd / Paypert (Բայբերդ), containing Armenian berd ('fortress'), Hellenized by Procopius as Baiberdon and adapted into Turkish as Bayburt.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Procopius, De Aedificiis (c. 550s CE); Movses Khorenatsi
older_name_by_867.notes: Movses of Khoren also mentions an earlier name Smbatapert.

b_keltzine.first_mention_attestation: Region attested in Strabo's Geographica (XI.4.8, XI.14.16, c. 23 CE) as Acilisene (Ἀκιλισηνή), later called Keltzene (Κελτζηνή) in Byzantine sources (e.g. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, De Administrando Imperio).
b_keltzine.etymology_analysis: Byzantine Greek Keltzēnē (Κελτζηνή) / Kelezēnē, evolved from Classical Acilisene (Armenian Ekełeac'), which also gave its name to the Kelkit river and town.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica (XI.4.8, c. 23 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Acilisene was the Classical form before Byzantine Keltzene.

b_trani.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Turenum in the Tabula Peutingeriana (4th century CE, based on 3rd-century Roman itinerary), and as an episcopal see at the Roman Council of 501 CE.
b_trani.etymology_analysis: From Roman Latin Turenum (recorded on the Tabula Peutingeriana), which contracted to medieval Trani.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tabula Peutingeriana (4th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Turenum is the earliest attested Roman name for Trani.

b_siponto.first_mention_attestation: Ancient port of Magna Graecia (Greek Sipious / Σιπιούς, Latin Sipontum), colonized by Rome in 194 BCE (Livy), with a bishopric attested by 465 CE.
b_siponto.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Sipious (Σιπιούς) and Latin Sipontum, evolving into Italian Siponto; abandoned after 13th-century earthquakes in favor of Manfredonia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Livy (Roman colony 194 BCE); Strabo
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek Sipious / Roman Sipontum.

b_venosa.first_mention_attestation: Captured by the Romans in 291 BCE after the Third Samnite War and established as the Roman colony of Venusia.
b_venosa.etymology_analysis: From Latin Venusia (associated by the Romans with the goddess Venus, Greek Aphrodisia), evolving into Italian Venosa.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman colonization records (291 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman colony of Venusia, birthplace of Horace (65 BCE).

b_acerenza.first_mention_attestation: Conquered by the Romans in 318 BCE as Aceruntia / Acheruntia / Acherontia, and attested as an episcopal see from 499 CE.
b_acerenza.etymology_analysis: From ancient Italic/Latin Aceruntia or Acherontia, which developed regularly into Italian Acerenza.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman conquest records (318 BCE); Horace
older_name_by_867.notes: Also famous as an Ostrogothic/Byzantine fortress in the Gothic Wars.

b_bari.first_mention_attestation: Harbor of Barium mentioned as early as 181 BCE (Livy), originally a Peucetian/Messapic settlement (Greek Barion / Βάριον), with a bishop attested at the Council of Sardica (347 CE).

morphemes.translation: house / settlement (Messapic etymology preserved in Etymologicum Magnum)

b_bari.etymology_analysis: From Messapic (preserved in the Etymologicum Magnum as meaning 'house'), Hellenized as Barion (Βάριον) and Latinized as Barium, yielding modern Bari.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Livy (181 BCE); Etymologicum Magnum
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Iapygian/Peucetian port.

b_matera.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE, III.105) as Mateola, and later mentioned in 867 CE during Emperor Louis II's campaign against the Saracens.

morphemes.translation: ancient town name (possibly from Messapic/Greek Met-Hera)

b_matera.etymology_analysis: Derived from Roman Mateola (Pliny), evolving into medieval Matera (though folk etymologies also link it to Greek Met-Hera).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Mateola.

b_taranto.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 706 BCE by Dorian Spartan colonists as Taras (Τάρας), later Roman Tarentum (captured 272 BCE).

morphemes.translation: named after mythical hero Taras (son of Poseidon)

b_taranto.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Taras (Τάρας, genitive Tarantos), named after the mythical hero Taras; Latinized as Tarentum, yielding Italian Taranto.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Greek foundation tradition (706 BCE); Herodotus; Strabo
older_name_by_867.notes: Greek Taras -> Latin Tarentum -> Italian Taranto.

b_lecce.first_mention_attestation: Messapian settlement conquered by Rome in the 3rd century BCE (c. 267–250 BCE) and known in Latin as Lupiae (Strabo, Pliny).

morphemes.translation: ancient town name (Roman Lupiae -> medieval Licea / Lecce)

b_lecce.etymology_analysis: From Roman Latin Lupiae (also Greek Loupiai), which evolved through medieval Licea/Litium into modern Italian Lecce.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica; Roman 3rd-century BCE conquest
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Messapian settlement, Roman Lupiae.

b_brindisi.first_mention_attestation: Messapian settlement (Brention) conquered by the Romans in 267 BCE and made a Latin colony (Brundisium) in 245–244 BCE.

morphemes.translation: deer's head (referring to the shape of the natural harbor)

b_brindisi.etymology_analysis: From Messapic Brention ('deer's head', describing the branched natural harbor), via Greek Brentesion (Βρεντέσιον) and Latin Brundisium, to Italian Brindisi.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman conquest (267 BCE); Strabo, Geographica
older_name_by_867.notes: Major Roman Adriatic port at the terminus of the Via Appia.

b_orlanto.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Pseudo-Scylax's Periplus (c. 350 BCE, §§1.14, 1.27) as Hydrous (Ὑδροῦς), and in Livy (191 BCE) and Strabo as Hydruntum.
b_orlanto.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Hydrous (Ὑδροῦς, 'abounding in water') and Latin Hydruntum, which evolved into Italian Otranto.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pseudo-Scylax, Periplus (c. 350 BCE); Livy (191 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek Hydrous -> Latin Hydruntum -> Italian Otranto.

b_mosynopolis.first_mention_attestation: The Byzantine name Mosynopolis first appears in 879–880 CE (Fourth Council of Constantinople); preceded on the same site by Roman Maximianopolis / Porsulis (4th century CE, c. 350 CE).
b_mosynopolis.etymology_analysis: Byzantine Greek Mosynopolis (Μοσυνόπολις), possibly from mosyn ('wooden tower') + polis ('city'), replacing the earlier imperial name Maximianopolis in the 9th century.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 4th-century Roman sources; Council of Ephesus (431 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Maximianopolis until the 9th century, when it became Mosynopolis.

b_xanthia.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as Xantheia (Ξάνθεια) in Strabo's Geographica (Book VII Fragments, c. 23 CE); later recorded in 879 CE (Bishop Georgios of Xantheia at the Fourth Council of Constantinople).
b_xanthia.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Xantheia (Ξάνθεια), attested by Strabo in Thrace, later Xanthē (Ξάνθη); traditionally linked to the Oceanid or Amazon Xanthi.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica Book VII Fragments (c. 23 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Strabo's Xantheia is identified with medieval/modern Xanthi.

b_traianopolis.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Roman Emperor Trajan (r. 98–117 CE) near ancient Doriscus; became capital and metropolitan see of the province of Rhodope in the 4th century CE.
b_traianopolis.etymology_analysis: From Greek Traianoupolis (Τραϊανούπολις, 'City of Trajan'), named after its founder, Emperor Trajan (r. 98–117 CE).

b_thasos.first_mention_attestation: Colonized by Greeks from Paros led by Telesicles c. 680–650 BCE (Archilochus; Herodotus).

morphemes.translation: island name (traditionally linked to mythical Phoenician prince Thasus)

b_thasos.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Thasos (Θάσος), name of the northern Aegean island and its main polis; Greek myth attributed it to the Phoenician hero Thasus.

b_rodopi.first_mention_attestation: Mount Rhodope (Ῥοδόπη) is first attested in Herodotus's Histories (Book IV.49, c. 440 BCE); later gave its name to the late Roman/early Byzantine province of Rhodope (4th century CE).

morphemes.translation: Rhodope (mountain range name, possibly 'rosy-faced' in Greek folk etymology)

b_rodopi.etymology_analysis: Ancient Thracian oronym Hellenized as Rhodopē (Ῥοδόπη), attested since Herodotus (5th century BCE) and used as a Roman/Byzantine provincial name.

b_serres.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Herodotus's Histories (5th century BCE, c. 440 BCE) as Siris (Σίρις), later Sirra (Theopompus), Sirae (Livy), and Serrae (Σέρραι) by the 5th century CE.
b_serres.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek Paeonian/Thracian toponym recorded as Siris by Herodotus, pluralized as Latin Sirae and Byzantine Greek Serrai (Σέρραι), yielding modern Serres.

current_repo_state.name: Sêrres
current_repo_state.b_origin: Serres / Siris (ancient inland Paeonian and Byzantine fortress) (in-game: Sêrres)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Inland fortress of Serres disambiguated from coastal port Goltstat / Chrysopolis.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Herodotus, Histories (5th century BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Singular Siris / Sirra became plural Sirae / Serrai by the 5th century CE.

b_siderokastron.first_mention_attestation: Fortress (Issari Fort) built by Byzantine Emperor Basil II in the early 11th century (c. 1014 CE) and named Siderokastron; no confirmed written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_siderokastron.etymology_analysis: Byzantine Greek Sidērokastron (Σιδηρόκαστρον, 'Iron Castle'), calqued into Ottoman Turkish as Demir Hisar; modern Greek Sidirokastro.

current_repo_state.name: Îsenburch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Descriptive Byzantine fortress toponym calqued to Tarraconian Îsenburch.

b_drama.first_mention_attestation: Ancient settlement Hydrama / Dyrama (later associated with Drabescus), attested as a small fortified settlement in the early Christian period (4th–7th centuries CE) tied to Philippi.
b_drama.etymology_analysis: Derived from Ancient Greek Hydrama (Ὕδραμα) or Dyrama ('rich in water'), which contracted over time into Drama.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Early Christian / classical Macedonian sources
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Hydrama / Dyrama; sometimes associated with Thracian Drabescus.

b_kavala.first_mention_attestation: The name Kavala emerged in the late 15th–early 16th century CE (c. 1500 CE); preceded on the same site by ancient Neapolis (c. 500 BCE) and Byzantine Christoupolis (early 9th century CE).

morphemes.translation: horse / relay station (uncertain; possibly from Italian cavallo or ancient Skavala)

b_kavala.etymology_analysis: Modern name Kavala emerged in the late medieval/Ottoman period, replacing Byzantine Christoupolis ('City of Christ', attested 8th c. CE) and ancient Neapolis ('New City').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Greek / New Testament (Acts 16:11); 8th-century Byzantine Notitiae
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Neapolis became Byzantine Christoupolis by the 8th century CE.

b_chrysopolis.first_mention_attestation: Chrysopolis at the mouth of the Strymon is first attested in written sources in the 10th century CE (fortified 9th–10th century CE); preceded by ancient Eion (attested c. 430 BCE).
b_chrysopolis.etymology_analysis: Greek Chrysopolis (Χρυσόπολις, 'Golden City'), a Byzantine port city built on the site of ancient Eion at the mouth of the Strymon River.

current_repo_state.name: Goltstat
current_repo_state.b_origin: Chrysopolis (Greek Chryso-polis, 'Golden City' on the Aegean) (in-game: Goltstat)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Ancient Greek trading emporium and port Chrysopolis disambiguated from inland Serres.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Eion was the predecessor of Byzantine Chrysopolis.

b_polygyros.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a chrysobull of Byzantine Emperor Nikephoros III Botaneiates c. 1080 CE; post-867 CE.
b_polygyros.etymology_analysis: Greek Polygyros (Πολύγυρος), variously derived from poly + geros ('very strong/healthy'), poly + hieros ('many temples'), or a personal name Polyaros; first attested c. 1080 CE.

older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Apollonia lay nearby, but Polygyros itself is first attested in 1080 CE.

b_rendina.first_mention_attestation: Fortress of Rentina is attested in Late Byzantine sources (e.g., John Kantakouzenos's History for 1334 CE); while the pass was used earlier, the name Rentina is post-867 CE.

morphemes.translation: medieval fortress name in the Mygdonian pass

b_rendina.etymology_analysis: Medieval Byzantine Greek Rentina (Ρεντίνα), attested as a strategic fortress on the Via Egnatia in the Late Byzantine period.

b_kassandreia.first_mention_attestation: Originally Potidaea (Ποτίδαια), founded by Corinthians c. 600 BCE; refounded as Cassandreia (Κασσάνδρεια) in 316 BCE by Cassander of Macedon.
b_kassandreia.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Kassandreia (Κασσάνδρεια), named after its founder Cassander of Macedon in 316 BCE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Herodotus; Thucydides (Corinthian foundation c. 600 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Potidaea was refounded by Cassander as Cassandreia in 316 BCE.

b_ierrisos.first_mention_attestation: The Byzantine see/name Ierissos (Erissos) is first definitively attested in 883 CE; preceded on the same site by ancient Greek Acanthus (Akanthos, founded c. 655 BCE).

morphemes.translation: possibly from Latin ericius ('hedgehog/thorn', translating Greek akanthos 'thorn')

b_ierrisos.etymology_analysis: Byzantine Greek Ierissos (Ἱερισσός), attested from 883 CE, possibly a Latinized translation (ericius 'spiny/thorny') of the ancient Greek name Acanthus (akanthos 'thorn').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Greek foundation (c. 655 BCE); Herodotus; Thucydides
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Acanthus was succeeded by Byzantine Ierissos (attested 883 CE).

b_thessaloniki.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 315 BCE by Cassander of Macedon and named after his wife Thessalonike, half-sister of Alexander the Great.
b_thessaloniki.etymology_analysis: Named after Princess Thessalonike of Macedon, whose name means 'Thessalian victory' (commemorating Philip II's victory in Thessaly on the day of her birth).

older_name_by_867.notes: Founded in 315 BCE by synoecism of 26 neighboring villages including Therma.

b_gynaikokastron.first_mention_attestation: Built in 1334 CE by Byzantine Emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos to defend Thessaloniki against the Serbs; post-867 CE.
b_gynaikokastron.etymology_analysis: Byzantine Greek Gynaikokastron (Γυναικόκαστρον, 'Women's Castle'), calqued into Ottoman Turkish as Avret Hisar; built in 1334 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Vrouwenburch
current_repo_state.b_origin: Gynaikokastron (Greek Gynaiko-kastron, 'Women's Castle / Queen's Castle') (in-game: Vrouwenburch)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Descriptive Byzantine fortress toponym calqued to Tarraconian Vrouwenburch.

b_langades.first_mention_attestation: Modern town of Lagkadas (Ottoman Langaza) has no confirmed written attestation <= 867 CE (ancient Lete lay nearby in Mygdonia).
b_langades.etymology_analysis: From Greek lagkadi ('valley, hollow'), plural/augmented Lagkadas (Λαγκαδάς); Ottoman Langaza.

older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Lete was nearby, but Lagkadas itself is post-867 CE.

b_mavrouda.first_mention_attestation: Small village in Volvi municipality (Thessaloniki regional unit) with no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_mavrouda.etymology_analysis: Greek Mavrouda (Μαυρούδα), derived from mavros ('black/dark'), likely from a personal name or dark soil/forest.

b_veria.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Thucydides's History of the Peloponnesian War for 432 BCE as Beroea (Βέροια).

morphemes.translation: ancient city name (possibly 'bearing/fertile' or named after mythical Beroe)

b_veria.etymology_analysis: Ancient Macedonian/Greek Beroia (Βέροια), Latinized as Beroea, evolving phonetically into modern Greek Veria (Βέροια).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War (432 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Continuous settlement since antiquity.

b_maglen.first_mention_attestation: Medieval fortress and region of Moglena (Μογλενά) is first attested in the early 11th century (captured by Basil II from the First Bulgarian Empire in 1015 CE; bishopric attested in 1020 CE); post-867 CE.
b_maglen.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic mŭgla ('fog, mist'), yielding Bulgarian Mŭglen / Macedonian Meglen / Greek Moglena (Μογλενά); replaced the ancient regional name Almopia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Thucydides (Almopia); early Byzantine Enotia
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Almopia was renamed Enotia in the early Byzantine period before Slavic Moglena (attested 1015 CE).

b_sthlanitza.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 11th century (c. 1020 CE) as Slanitsa / Sthlanitza (Σθλάνιτζα), an eparchy of the Archbishopric of Ohrid; post-867 CE.
b_sthlanitza.etymology_analysis: South Slavic Slanitsa, Hellenized as Sthlanitza (Σθλάνιτζα), attested as an 11th-century bishopric in the plain of Giannitsa.

b_voden.first_mention_attestation: The Slavic name Vodĭnŭ (Водьнъ) / Voden is first attested in the 10th century CE (post-867 CE), though the ancient city of Edessa on the same site dates to antiquity.
b_voden.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic Vodĭnŭ ('place of water', from voda 'water'), referencing the waterfalls of Edessa; used in Greek as Vodena until 1923.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ancient Macedonian tradition; Roman inscriptions & mint (27 BCE–268 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Edessa ('tower in the water') was renamed Vodĭnŭ / Voden by the 10th century CE and restored to Edessa in 1923.

b_kalyvia.first_mention_attestation: Modern village in Skydra municipality (Pella regional unit) with no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_kalyvia.etymology_analysis: From Greek kalývia (Καλύβια, 'huts'), a common modern Greek settlement name for seasonal pastoral or agricultural hamlets.
